sections.text:
Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action.

To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting.

Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction.

AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.

summary.en: The paper presents AWAM, an active-perception method that plans where to observe and imagines views along a planned trajectory before manipulation. Task-related virtual camera motion queries a geometry-conditioned world model to create a reusable spatial prior, which is compressed into fixed memory and fused with live observations for diffusion-based action prediction. The authors report competitive success rates on LIBERO-Occ, LIBERO-Plus, RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and real-robot trials, supporting improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts.
summary.zh: 论文提出 AWAM，一种在操作前主动规划观察位置、并沿计划轨迹想象视野的主动感知方法。它用任务相关的虚拟相机运动查询几何条件世界模型，生成可复用空间先验，再将压缩后的固定记忆与实时观测融合，通过扩散模型预测动作。作者报告其在 LIBERO-Occ、LIBERO-Plus、RLBench-OG Occlusion1 和真实机器人试验中取得有竞争力的成功率，并称结果表明该方法在所评估的遮挡与分布变化下更稳健。

sections.text:
Zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) requires robots to find target objects in unseen environments without task-specific fine-tuning or pre-built maps, a key capability for general-purpose service robots.

Yet methods that perform well in simulation often degrade in cluttered real-world scenes with severe occlusion and latent hazards, where large unseen regions make single-scene inference brittle and unsafe. We propose Schr\"odinger's Navigator, a belief-aware framework that reasons at inference time over multiple trajectory-conditioned imagined 3D futures.

Given candidate paths, a trajectory-conditioned 3D world model predicts hypothetical observations and maintains a superposition of plausible scene realizations rather than committing to one map.

An adaptive occluder-aware sampler directs imagination to uncertainty-critical regions, while a Future-Aware Value Map (FAVM) aggregates imagined futures for robust, proactive action selection.

Experiments in simulation and on a physical Go2 quadruped show that Schr\"odinger's Navigator outperforms strong ZSON baselines, improving hidden-target discovery and risk-aware waypoint selection in occlusion-heavy navigation scenarios.

These results highlight imagined 3D futures as a scalable and generalizable strategy for zero-shot navigation in uncertain real-world environments.

summary.en: The paper introduces Schrödinger’s Navigator for zero-shot object navigation without task-specific fine-tuning or pre-built maps. For candidate paths, it imagines multiple trajectory-conditioned 3D futures, uses an uncertainty-aware occluder sampler to focus on critical regions, and aggregates futures in a value map for action selection. The authors report that experiments in simulation and on a physical Go2 quadruped outperform the compared ZSON baselines, improving hidden-target discovery and risk-aware waypoint selection in occlusion-heavy scenarios.
summary.zh: 论文提出 Schrödinger’s Navigator，用于无需任务专门微调或预建地图的零样本目标导航。该方法针对候选路径想象多个轨迹条件化的三维未来，并以不确定性感知的遮挡采样器聚焦关键区域，再通过未来感知价值图汇总结果以选择行动。作者报告，仿真和实体 Go2 四足机器人实验显示，该方法优于所比较的零样本导航基线，并改善遮挡场景中的隐藏目标发现和风险感知航点选择。

items.title: Schr\"odinger's Navigator: Imagining an Ensemble of Futures for Zero-Shot Object Navigation

sections.text:
Heterogeneous robot teams enable complex, long-horizon tasks by combining complementary sensing, mobility, and manipulation capabilities across multiple embodiments.

Yet existing systems struggle to retain execution-time corrections as reusable experience, maintain task-relevant context memory across space and time for reliable handoffs, and explicitly represent the inter-robot dependencies required for structured collaboration.

In order to address these challenges, we present InstAgent, a recursively self-improving (RSI) Agent Operating System for heterogeneous robot collaboration. InstAgent organizes team behaviors as agentic behavior trees (BTs) that explicitly model capability assignment, inter-robot dependencies and handoff checks.

The RSI mechanism updates these collaboration programs from execution feedback and preserves successful revisions for reuse in future tasks, while shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory provides context for planning and handoff validation.

Experiments on 20 real-world multi-robot tasks with three high-level models show consistent gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.

summary.en: The paper presents InstAgent, a recursively self-improving agent operating system for heterogeneous robot collaboration. It organizes team behaviors as agentic behavior trees that represent capability assignment, inter-robot dependencies, and handoff checks. Execution feedback updates collaboration programs, and successful revisions are retained for future tasks; shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory supports planning and handoff validation. The authors report consistent gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency across 20 real-world multi-robot tasks involving three high-level models.
summary.zh: 论文提出 InstAgent，一个用于异构机器人协作的递归自我改进智能体操作系统。它以智能体行为树组织团队行为，显式表示能力分配、机器人间依赖和交接检查；系统根据执行反馈更新协作程序，并保存成功修订以供后续任务复用。共享的多模态时空记忆为规划和交接验证提供上下文。作者报告，在由三种高层模型参与的 20 项真实世界多机器人任务实验中，任务成功率、首次完成率和执行效率均持续提升。

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as $\pi_{0.5}$, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising.

We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of $\pi_{0.5}$, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert.

Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence.

To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block.

MambaAct uses a $10\times$ smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by $64.8\%$ on LIBERO and $58.8\%$ in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by $1.08$ percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks.

Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.

summary.en: The paper presents MambaAct, replacing the Transformer action expert in a flow-matching vision-language-action policy with a compact Mamba expert while retaining the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder. A Context Compressor turns prefix tokens into a compact signal that modulates Mamba blocks. The authors report a tenfold smaller action expert, denoising latency reductions of 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real-world deployment, and a 1.08 percentage-point increase in mean LIBERO success. They also report gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks.
summary.zh: 论文提出 MambaAct，用紧凑的 Mamba 动作专家替换流匹配视觉语言动作策略中的 Transformer 动作专家，同时保留预训练视觉语言前缀编码器。上下文压缩器将前缀词元转为调制 Mamba 模块的紧凑条件信号。作者报告，动作专家规模缩小十倍；在 LIBERO 和真实部署中，去噪延迟分别降低 64.8% 和 58.8%，LIBERO 平均成功率提高 1.08 个百分点，并称在其他基准上保持提升。

sections.text:
When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses.

We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: （1） Does memory provide a net benefit? （2） Under what conditions does memory help? （3） Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? （4） Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts?

At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory.

In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements.

To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions.

These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.

summary.en: The paper proposes IMEP, an intervention protocol for evaluating memory in vision-language-action systems. It separates decision correctness from motor execution and compares target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place intervention, including installation, changed 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes; changing key facts showed no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. The authors introduce ChainBench, where full memory raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions.
summary.zh: 论文提出视觉语言动作系统的干预式记忆评估协议 IMEP，区分决策正确性与动作执行成功，并通过替换目标事实、保留事实的替换、微小数值扰动和精确复制来检验记忆作用。跨回合学习记忆库实验中，包含安装过程的一单位末位干预改变了 11.9% 的成对结果，而关键事实替换未显示出超出保留事实替换的明确效果。作者还提出 ChainBench；完整记忆配置将任务成功率从 39.1% 提高到 74.3%，与共享记录执行下的预言机决策条件相当。

sections.text:
We demonstrate high-precision global localization using natural ground texture viewed through microscope optics, achieving localization in the tens-of-micrometers regime. For the planar ground texture localization problem considered here, we relate optical magnification and image-space localization uncertainty to physical localization precision.

Leveraging this relationship, we then develop a microscope-based localization system that addresses the calibration, camera-modeling, and focus challenges introduced by high-magnification imaging. We evaluate this system across several surface textures using a calibrated precision gantry.

Across 1,007 held-out queries per surface, the system localizes every query and achieves translation RMSEs of 28$-$73 $\mu$m. Independent photometric registration agrees with the feature-based localization estimates to within approximately 9 $\mu$m RMSE.

We further demonstrate localization on a low-cost mobile robot using the gantry-collected maps, and also show that the system can resolve micrometer-scale displacement caused by thermal expansion.

These results show that microscopic natural surface texture can bring mobile localization into a precision regime typically associated with fixed positioning systems.

summary.en: The paper studies global mobile robot localization from natural ground texture imaged through microscope optics and relates magnification and image-space uncertainty to planar localization precision. The authors build a system addressing calibration, camera modeling, and focus at high magnification, then evaluate it on several surfaces using a precision gantry. All 1,007 held-out queries per surface are localized, with translation RMSEs of 28–73 micrometers. Independent photometric registration agrees within about 9 micrometers RMSE. The authors also demonstrate localization on a low-cost robot and detection of micrometer-scale thermal expansion displacement.
summary.zh: 论文研究利用显微光学观察天然地面纹理进行移动机器人全局定位，并分析光学放大率、图像定位不确定性与平面定位精度的关系。作者开发了处理高倍率成像标定、相机建模和对焦问题的系统，并用精密龙门架评估多种表面纹理。每种表面上的1,007个留出查询均成功定位，平移均方根误差为28–73微米；独立光度配准结果与特征定位结果的均方根差约为9微米。作者还展示了低成本移动机器人定位和热膨胀导致的微米级位移检测。

sections.text:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide a natural language interface to robot control, but the mapping from language to behavior is often brittle and unintuitive: semantically similar instructions can induce drastically different behaviors, while some capabilities may not be elicitable through prompting alone.

As a result, both human instructions and zero-shot language models can fail to reliably steer VLAs toward successful task execution.

In this work, we propose a framework that interactively searches for language sequences that improve closed-loop VLA task performance, distills these sequences into a test-time language feedback policy (LFP), and learns an improvement head that predicts when language steering will improve performance.

We conformalize this improvement head to prevent harmful steering interventions, where the LFP decreases task performance relative to the original instruction on out-of-distribution scenarios.

Crucially, our approach operates on arbitrary frozen pre-trained VLAs, requiring neither access to the original training distribution nor fine-tuning of the underlying model. On seen environments, our conformalized LFP improves base VLA performance by 24.7% in simulation and 65.0% in hardware.

On visual and semantic perturbations with calibration samples, our conformalized LFP has strong harmlessness guarantees, and produces recovery behaviors not observed with open-loop prompting.

summary.en: The paper proposes interactively searching for language sequences that improve closed-loop task performance of vision-language-action models, distilling them into a test-time language feedback policy, and training a head to predict when steering will help. Conformalization is used to reduce harmful interventions on out-of-distribution scenarios. The method is designed for arbitrary frozen pretrained VLAs without access to their original training distribution or model fine-tuning. In seen environments, the authors report improvements of 24.7% in simulation and 65.0% in hardware. With calibration samples, they report strong harmlessness guarantees under visual and semantic perturbations and recovery behaviors absent from open-loop prompting.
summary.zh: 论文提出一种为视觉—语言—动作模型寻找有效语言序列的方法，并将其提炼为测试时语言反馈策略，同时训练改进预测头判断何时进行语言引导。该方法通过保形化降低分布外场景中引导反而损害任务表现的风险，可用于任意冻结的预训练模型，无需原始训练分布或微调底层模型。在已见环境中，作者报告策略使基础模型表现于仿真提升24.7%、硬件提升65.0%。对于带校准样本的视觉和语义扰动，作者称其具有较强的无害性保证，并能产生开放环提示未观察到的恢复行为。

sections.text:
Generalist robot policies offer strong behavioral priors, but achieving deployment-level reliability and throughput remains difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these policies, yet its effectiveness is constrained by the cost of online interaction.

Existing methods adapt frozen flow-matching policies by treating noise space as a continuous action space. We show that this behaviorally unstructured space makes exploration inefficient, often preventing these methods from extracting meaningful learning signals on challenging tasks.

We introduce AnchorQ, which enables coarse-to-fine policy improvement through a structured, refinable latent action representation. At each decision step, AnchorQ uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, samples local particles around those anchors, and applies value-guided sampling to explore promising refinements.

Our analysis shows that anchors reduce identification complexity at the cost of support bias; particle refinement trades this bias against action-class complexity; and critic accuracy determines the reliability of KL-regularized, value-guided selection.

Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, AnchorQ outperforms state-of-the-art post-training baselines in sample efficiency, delivering a 37% improvement in real-world success rate and 97% higher simulated task throughput under the same interaction budget. Additional visualizations are available on our website https://anchorq-rl.com/.

summary.en: The paper introduces AnchorQ, which uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent action anchors, samples nearby particles, and applies value-guided refinement to improve frozen flow-matching policies. The authors analyze trade-offs involving anchor support bias, particle refinement, and critic accuracy. In simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, they report better sample efficiency than post-training baselines under the same interaction budget, including a 37% improvement in real-world success rate and 97% higher simulated task throughput.
summary.zh: 论文提出 AnchorQ，通过流反演将参考行为映射为依赖状态的潜在动作锚点，在锚点附近采样并依据价值引导细化，以提升冻结流匹配策略的强化学习效率。作者分析了锚点、粒子细化与评论家准确度之间的权衡。仿真和真实操作任务结果显示，在相同交互预算下，该方法优于后训练基线；作者报告真实成功率提高37%，仿真任务吞吐量提高97%。

sections.text:
Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge.

Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics.

We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations.

We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels.

On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing 225 consecutive $\mathbf{180^\circ}$ rotations (112.5 full rotations) at $\sim0.36 \;\text{rot/s}$ in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information.

Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important. This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used.

By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.

summary.en: The paper studies blind Baoding ball rotation with a Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback. The authors report zero-shot transfer using a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware simulated embodiment, tactile calibration, and two episodic domain randomizations. In one continuous physical-hand trial, the policy completed 225 consecutive 180-degree rotations, or 112.5 full rotations, at about 0.36 rotations per second, without vision or object-state information. The paper also evaluates tactile sensing against proprioception alone and identifies important hand regions.

sections.text:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through cooperation.

Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve, a framework that represents team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills.

CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded execution parameters.

Physical verification evaluates each executed transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors.

Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families, CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end success.

Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and contact stability.

These results support executable coordination as a practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under shared physical constraints.

summary.en: CoEvolve represents multi-robot coordination as executable code over fixed motor skills and revises strategies based on physical verification, retaining accepted experience. A multimodal model instantiates strategies using motion primitives, objectives, temporary roles, and bounded parameters. Evaluation used two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids carrying a rigid payload through constrained corridors. Across 15 base runs, 8 tasks were completed, and each of three multimodal backbone families achieved end-to-end success. Further evaluations reported verified placement on two additional layouts and with same- or cross-backbone experience initialization, while identifying limits in motion precision and contact stability.

sections.text:
Planning while moving faces an historical trade-off between deliberation and reactivity. A planner running concurrently with execution needs time to compute, so the robot must commit to an open-loop action chunk for that duration: a longer commitment buys a better plan at the cost of feedback frequency.

Existing controllers fix this action commitment, and consequently the computation budget, before deployment.

However, the optimal computation time is highly state-dependent (due to factors such as unmodeled dynamics, safety constraints, and marginal optimisation gains), i.e. dynamic, therefore offline static tuning risks leaving systems blind during critical maneuvers or unable to find global effective solutions.

We cast the identification of the optimal computation budget as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) in which a single decision defines both the robot action commitments and the time allocated to the solver. To solve this, we train a reinforcement-learning policy conditioned on the current state, the executing plan, and inexpensive planner statistics.

Across ground-robot navigation, agile quadrotor flight, and contact-rich manipulation, the learned policy changes its budget with the demands of the scenario, discovering efficient reasoning patterns that outperform fixed-budget baselines. https://lorenzomagnino.github.io/learning-robot-metareasoning-review/

summary.en: The paper models computation-budget selection for planning during robot motion as a semi-Markov decision process: each decision sets both action commitment and solver time. The authors train a reinforcement-learning policy conditioned on the current state, executing plan, and inexpensive planner statistics. They argue that appropriate computation time varies with state and task demands, whereas fixed commitments constrain feedback frequency. Across ground-robot navigation, agile quadrotor flight, and contact-rich manipulation, the learned policy adapts its budget to scenario demands and is reported to outperform fixed-budget baselines.
summary.zh: 论文将机器人规划时的计算预算选择建模为半马尔可夫决策过程：每次决策同时确定动作持续时间和求解器计算时间。作者训练一个强化学习策略，根据当前状态、正在执行的计划及低成本规划器统计信息调整预算。研究指出，固定动作承诺会限制反馈频率，而合适的计算时间随状态和任务需求变化。在地面机器人导航、敏捷四旋翼飞行及接触丰富的操作任务中，学习策略会随场景调整预算，并报告其推理模式优于固定预算基线。

sections.text:
Jellyfish-inspired robots offer a compliant and efficient approach to underwater locomotion, but achieving large deformation together with repeatable actuation and closed-loop control remains challenging. In this work, we present a tendon-driven robotic jellyfish with constrained soft actuation.

Each actuator combines a flexible substrate with discrete constraints, enabling bending up to \(150^\circ\) with an approximately linear tendon displacement-bending relationship. Eight actuators driven by four servos allow the robot to perform stable swimming, attitude adjustment, and self-righting.

Based on the linear actuation, a reinforcement-learning controller is further developed, enabling closed-loop depth regulation in both simulation and physical experiments.

These results show that mechanical constraints can improve the controllability of soft actuation while preserving compliant jellyfish-like motion, providing a route toward manoeuvrable and autonomous jellyfish robots.

summary.en: The study presents a tendon-driven robotic jellyfish with constrained soft actuation. Each actuator combines a flexible substrate with discrete constraints, allowing bending up to 150 degrees and an approximately linear relationship between tendon displacement and bending. Eight actuators, driven by four servos, support stable swimming, attitude adjustment, and self-righting. Using the linear actuation, the authors develop a reinforcement-learning controller for closed-loop depth regulation, demonstrated in simulation and physical experiments. They state that mechanical constraints can improve soft-actuation controllability while preserving compliant jellyfish-like motion.

sections.text:
Humanoid behavior foundation models aim to acquire reusable whole-body control policies from broad human motion priors, enabling a single controller to produce diverse and expressive behaviors. However, existing motion-centric foundation policies largely assume that the reference motion is already physically compatible with the robot's surroundings.

This assumption breaks when the demonstrator, operator, and robot inhabit different environments: a human motion may specify the intended behavior, but not the footholds, clearance, body height, or contact timing required by the robot's local terrain.

We introduce \emph{Perceptive Behavior Foundation Model} (Perceptive BFM), a terrain-aware humanoid control framework that grounds human motion priors in robot-centric perception. The model preserves raw kinematic motion references as the behavioral interface, while using local terrain observations to adapt contacts, posture, and timing.

To provide scalable terrain supervision, we develop \emph{terrain-conformal reference synthesis} (TCRS), which converts locomotion-oriented human motion clips into terrain-consistent references through contact-aware foothold construction, foot-geometry-aware swing optimization, support-aware root reconstruction, collision repair, and multi-point inverse kinematics.

We then train a blind adapted-reference teacher and transfer its terrain-conformal behavior to a deployed raw-reference student through target-frame action alignment.

The student is an identity-gated Transformer tracker whose terrain features enter through residual pathways initialized to preserve the motion-tracking prior and trained to produce local corrections only when needed.

summary.en: Perceptive BFM combines human motion priors with robot-centric terrain perception to adapt contacts, posture, and timing to local conditions. For scalable terrain supervision, the authors introduce terrain-conformal reference synthesis, using contact-aware foothold construction, foot-geometry-aware swing optimization, support-aware root reconstruction, collision repair, and multi-point inverse kinematics. They train a blind adapted-reference teacher and transfer its behavior to a deployed raw-reference student through target-frame action alignment. The student is an identity-gated Transformer tracker whose terrain features enter through residual pathways, preserving the motion-tracking prior while enabling local corrections when needed.

sections.text:
Robotic systems for environmental monitoring and ecological surveying in wetlands and swamps must operate across diverse terrestrial and aquatic conditions. Conventional fixed-geometry wheels cannot adapt their contact geometry to these varying conditions.

This work presents MOSS (Multimodal Origami Swamp Robot System), a compact amphibious robotic platform with 3D-printed origami wheels. The compact crank mechanism switches the wheel between contracted and expanded configurations, changing its width, body diameter, and fin orientation simultaneously.

The contracted configuration is better suited to efficient rolling on firmer ground, whereas the expanded configuration provides greater contact and terrain engagement on softer surfaces. MOSS was evaluated on soil, sand, mud with varying water content, and water, in addition to in-motion morphing and terrestrial-aquatic transition tests.

The more energy-efficient wheel configuration depended on terrain. The contracted configuration achieved a lower cost of transport on firmer soil and mud, whereas the expanded configuration performed better on wetter mud, sand, and water, reducing the cost of transport by up to 29%.

Expanded wheels also reduced slip in wet mud and reduced both slip and hub sinkage in sand. MOSS successfully completed configuration changes in $1.95 \pm 0.11$ s and demonstrated continuous locomotion across soil-mud-water transitions. Outdoor trials further demonstrated operation across natural deformable terrain and water.

These results show that adaptive wheel geometry provides terrain-dependent locomotion benefits and enables a single compact platform to traverse substantially different terrestrial and aquatic conditions.

summary.en: The paper presents MOSS, a compact amphibious robot with 3D-printed origami wheels that switch between contracted and expanded shapes. The configurations change wheel width, body diameter, and fin orientation, with performance depending on terrain. Tests covered soil, sand, mud at varying water content, water, in-motion morphing, and land-water transitions. Expanded wheels reduced transport cost by up to 29% on wetter mud, sand, and water, and reduced slip in wet mud and sand. Outdoor trials demonstrated operation over natural deformable terrain and water.

sections.text:
Humanoid control requires coordinating whole-body posture with position and heading in the world frame. Mainstream controllers imitate trajectories in the root frame, but struggle to regain the target world pose after displacement.

We introduce BeJEPA, a goal-conditioned Behavior World Model learned through unsupervised reinforcement learning from human motion priors and robot interaction. BeJEPA learns a shared representation of body configuration and world placement through a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA).

A Dynamic Predictor predicts the next state embedding under an action, while a Successor Predictor summarizes a goal-conditioned policy's expected discounted future state embeddings in a single vector.

During joint training, Dynamic grounds the initial representation in observed physical transitions, while Successor increasingly organizes it around long-term behavior. Their composition guides policy improvement through one physical prediction and one behavioral summary, without long imagined rollouts.

In 20-second motion-tracking experiments, BeJEPA with online action refinement using Dynamic outperforms all evaluated baselines in global body-position error, reducing it on AMASS by 61.7% relative to BFM-Zero with world-pose inputs and 58.7% relative to SONIC.

Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates joint attainment of posture, world position, and heading goals, recovery from the ground, and closed-loop return after disturbances and goal changes. Project page: https://ylyem9x.github.io/BeJEPA-project.

summary.en: BeJEPA is a goal-conditioned behavior world model learned through unsupervised reinforcement learning from human motion priors and robot interaction. Its joint-embedding architecture uses a Dynamic Predictor for next-state embeddings and a Successor Predictor to summarize expected future embeddings for a goal-conditioned policy. In 20-second motion-tracking experiments, online action refinement with Dynamic outperformed the evaluated baselines on global body-position error, with reported reductions on AMASS of 61.7% and 58.7% relative to two specified baselines. A Unitree G1 deployment demonstrated goal attainment for posture, position, and heading, as well as recovery and return after disturbances.

We present LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300, a policy that combines a Human300-fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 action generator, an action-conditioned graph dynamics model, and a learned binary state-reward scorer.

At inference, the policy samples four action chunks, predicts the future latent features and robot state for each, and executes the candidate with the highest predicted-state reward logit. Predictions therefore influence the actions sent to the environment.

The evaluated system uses a 16-step prediction horizon and keeps all three components frozen during evaluation. In the local evaluation on 50 RoboCasa 1.0.1 tasks in the pretrain kitchen split, with 50 episodes per task, the system records 207/2,500 successes (8.28%), compared with 181/2,500 (7.24%) in the historical self-trained GR00T-N1.5 baseline.

The observed difference is 26 successes, or 1.04 percentage points. The atomic group improves from 141/900 to 150/900.Separately, the RoboCasa maintainers re-evaluated the submission and reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%) across 50 tasks, with leaderboard rates of 48.3%, 16.3%, and 3.1% for Atomic-Seen, Composite-Seen, and Composite-Unseen.

The local and official results are reported separately; their difference is not attributed to a model improvement. Recorded local audits identify 212,700 changed environment-input chunks, including 28,223 in atomic tasks. We describe the actual training stages, implemented inference mechanism, evaluation provenance, and public reproduction entrypoints.

These results document an active prediction-and-selection system and a positive historical difference.

summary.en: LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300 combines a Human300-fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 action generator, an action-conditioned graph dynamics model, and a binary state-reward scorer. At inference, it samples four action chunks, predicts future latent features and robot states, then selects the candidate with the highest predicted reward. All components remain frozen during evaluation. In a local evaluation of 50 tasks with 50 episodes each, it recorded 207/2,500 successes (8.28%), compared with 181/2,500 (7.24%) for a historical self-trained baseline. RoboCasa maintainers separately reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%); the authors do not attribute the difference between evaluations to model improvement.

sections.text:
Precise grounding matters. It specifies which object is the target and where that object is, even in clutter and for tiny objects, and it has to be fast enough for closed-loop control.

Yet vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) take perception from general-purpose vision-language and video-generation backbones, which still fail in these settings. We introduce GroundingPI, a 4B grounding foundation model that generates points and boxes as quantized coordinates in a shared vocabulary.

Training combines multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO, using supervision from public datasets and dedicated data engines.

Against 44 baselines across 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, GroundingPI establishes a new state of the art, averaging 73.68%, above the larger GPT-6 Astra (71.54%).As a downstream visual backbone, GroundingPI improves performance on robotic manipulation and autonomous driving.

On RoboTwin 2.0, it outperforms every mainstream backbone we evaluate in all four out-of-distribution settings, by up to 24.8% relative to the strongest backbone. On RoboCasa-GR1, GroundingPI trained with 50% of the demonstrations outperforms those baselines trained with 75%.

On nuScenes, used as the visual backbone, GroundingPI attains an average open-loop L2 error of 0.296 m. We systematically analyze GroundingPI's pretraining in scale and data composition. Downstream autonomous driving and robotic manipulation improve as the pretraining is scaled.

Analyzing the data recipe across these 11 perceptual capabilities shows dense grounding's substantial benefits for both, and OCR's potential as a catalyst for perceptual learning. These results support grounding as a perceptual foundation, and dedicated perceptual pretraining as a promising direction for foundation models of physical intelligence.

summary.en: The paper introduces GroundingPI, a 4B grounding foundation model that generates points and boxes as quantized coordinates in a shared vocabulary. Training combines multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO reinforcement learning. The authors report a 73.68% average across 34 grounding benchmarks, surpassing 44 baselines, and describe gains when using the model as a visual backbone for manipulation and driving. Evaluations include RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa-GR1, and nuScenes; the abstract does not claim real-world deployment.
summary.zh: 论文提出 GroundingPI，一种以量化坐标在共享词表中生成点和框的 4B grounding 基础模型，训练结合多模态与空间预训练、监督微调和 GRPO 强化学习。作者报告其在 34 项 grounding 基准上超过 44 个基线，平均成绩为 73.68%，并称其作为视觉骨干可改善机器人操作和自动驾驶表现。在 RoboTwin 2.0、RoboCasa-GR1 和 nuScenes 的评测结果，以及预训练规模与数据配方分析，均支持作者关于 grounding 可作为物理智能感知基础的主张；摘要未说明这些结果来自真实部署。

sections.text:
Quadruped parkour policies handle canonical obstacles well, but their training curricula often miss the irregular, compound geometry of industrial and disaster-response sites, where agile locomotion matters most.

Such environments pose a hard generalization problem: even training directly on reconstructed geometry from the target site does not reliably yield policies that traverse it. Hand-designed curricula span only a few terrain families, and recent LLM-generated curricula offer little control over which policy weaknesses they target.

We propose FCTS, a failure-conditioned terrain curriculum framework that uses localized traversal failures to automatically generate the terrains a policy should train on next.

Each failure's location, termination mode, robot state, and surrounding terrain geometry condition this generation, and Monte Carlo Tree Search explores alternative curriculum trajectories under a fixed training budget.

On terrains built from scanned real-world construction sites, FCTS raises success rate from 28.4% to 85.8% on a medium-difficulty course and from 14.9% to 44.7% on a hard course relative to the strongest parkour or LLM-curriculum baselines, and maintains higher progress on extreme terrains where full traversal is rare.

Hardware experiments on a quadruped robot confirm that the learned FCTS policies transfer to the real world.

summary.en: FCTS is a curriculum framework that generates future training terrains from localized traversal failures. Generation is conditioned on failure location, termination mode, robot state, and nearby terrain; Monte Carlo Tree Search explores curriculum trajectories under a fixed training budget. On terrains built from scanned construction sites, the authors report higher success rates than the strongest parkour or LLM-curriculum baselines on medium and hard courses, and greater progress on extreme terrain. Quadruped hardware experiments indicate that the learned policies transfer to the real world.
summary.zh: 论文提出 FCTS，一种依据局部行走失败自动生成后续训练地形的课程框架。系统利用失败位置、终止模式、机器人状态及周边地形条件生成，并通过蒙特卡洛树搜索探索课程路线。在由真实施工场地扫描数据构建的地形上，相较最强跑酷或语言模型课程基线，中等难度课程成功率从 28.4% 提升至 85.8%，高难度课程从 14.9% 提升至 44.7%；极端地形上的前进进度也更高。四足机器人硬件实验显示，学习到的策略可迁移至现实环境。

sections.text:
We present OrbiSim, a novel robotic simulation paradigm that redefines world models as a fully differentiable physics engine for embodied intelligence.

Unlike prior world models that focus on unconstrained imagination in latent or visual domains, OrbiSim establishes a unified, physically-grounded pathway that bridges structured scene assets, neural dynamics, and downstream reinforcement learning.

By enabling end-to-end differentiability throughout the entire simulation loop -- spanning from explicit state transitions to visual observation generation -- OrbiSim supports tasks traditionally intractable for classical simulators, such as differentiable contact modeling, gradient-based policy optimization under sparse rewards, and intuitive physical inference.

Empirical results demonstrate that OrbiSim significantly outperforms state-of-the-art world models in both predictive fidelity and control performance. Furthermore, its consistent responsiveness to asset configurations and physical parameters suggests its potential as a differentiable tool for enhancing robot simulation and policy training.

summary.en: OrbiSim is presented as a fully differentiable physics-engine paradigm for embodied intelligence, connecting structured scene assets, neural dynamics, and downstream reinforcement learning. Differentiability spans state transitions and visual observation generation, with intended applications including contact modeling, gradient-based policy optimization under sparse rewards, and physical inference. The authors state that empirical results show better predictive fidelity and control performance than state-of-the-art world models. They also report responsiveness to asset configurations and physical parameters, suggesting potential use in robot simulation and policy training; specific experimental details are not given.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable language-guided robot manipulation, but remain vulnerable to visual attacks that undermine user control over robot behavior. Prior studies optimize visual perturbations using fixed target supervision. However, the perturbation can change earlier actions and, in turn, the physical states reached later.

As the attacked trajectory evolves, this supervision may no longer match the behavior needed at the states actually reached. Accurately matching these targets can therefore fail to advance the attacker-specified task. Even with suitable supervision, reducing average matching error does not ensure sustained task progress.

The robot may still fail at a critical stage, and further updates can disrupt previously successful behavior. To address these limitations, we propose TRACO, a framework that enhances existing targeted visual attacks through closed-loop optimization.

Its Execution-Driven Supervision rebuilds supervision for the states reached under attack to guide subsequent updates. Within this framework, Progress-Guided Selection focuses updates where progress stalls while maintaining supervision on the earlier behavior needed to reach that point.

Experiments across VLA models and simulation environments show improved task-redirection success with TRACO, highlighting the security implications of closed-loop attack optimization.

summary.en: The paper presents TRACO, a closed-loop optimization framework for improving targeted visual attacks on vision-language-action models. Execution-Driven Supervision rebuilds guidance based on states actually reached under attack, while Progress-Guided Selection directs updates to stalled progress and preserves supervision for earlier behavior needed to reach that point. The authors argue that fixed target supervision can become mismatched as trajectories change, and that lower average matching error does not ensure task progress. Experiments across VLA models and simulation environments show improved task-redirection success and highlight security implications.
summary.zh: 论文研究视觉语言动作模型中的视觉任务重定向攻击，并提出 TRACO，通过闭环优化改进已有的定向视觉攻击。其执行驱动监督会依据攻击轨迹实际到达的状态重建监督信号；进度引导选择则把更新集中在进展停滞处，同时维持到达该处所需的先前行为监督。作者指出，固定目标监督可能与后续状态不匹配，降低平均误差也不保证持续推进。跨 VLA 模型和仿真环境的实验显示，TRACO 提高了任务重定向成功率，并揭示闭环攻击优化的安全影响。

sections.text:
Reliable vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires not only understanding instructions but also determining whether and how a robot can physically execute them. However, existing VLN benchmarks typically assume executable instructions and focus on long-horizon tasks.

This leaves body-dependent local execution, including passability and collision-free execution, largely unexamined. Evaluating these factors within long-horizon tasks would entangle local physical execution with task planning and long-term spatial memory, making navigation failures difficult to attribute.

We therefore focus on grounding local navigation commands in executable motion under environmental and robot body constraints. We present PASS-VLN, a passability-aware local-command VLN benchmark and model.

The benchmark holds the scene, instruction, start pose, and reference route fixed while varying robot body width, requiring target completion when the instructed passage is feasible and stopping before blockage otherwise.

Our model encodes body width through obstacle inflation in a depth-derived local bird's-eye view, fuses geometry with visual and linguistic context, and predicts discrete latent action codes for continuous closed-loop execution.

Experiments show that PASS-VLN improves collision-free success by approximately 12 percentage points over a strong VLN model fine-tuned on our benchmark, while adapting reach-versus-stop behavior to body constraints and generalizing to unseen body widths.

When integrated with a high-level planner, PASS-VLN achieves higher success with fewer local commands, while real-world deployment further demonstrates its effectiveness as a low-level executor. The benchmark and model will be released.

summary.en: The paper presents PASS-VLN, a passability-aware benchmark and model for grounding local vision-and-language navigation commands in executable motion. The benchmark fixes the scene, instruction, start pose, and route while varying robot width, requiring arrival when a passage is feasible and stopping when blocked. The model encodes width through obstacle inflation in a depth-derived local bird’s-eye view. Experiments report about a 12-point improvement in collision-free success over a strong benchmark-fine-tuned VLN model, adaptation to unseen widths, and effectiveness in planner integration and real-world deployment.

sections.text:
Robot policies map observations to actions, typically using multilayer perceptrons (MLPs).Yet robot dynamics and control objectives involve multiplicative interactions among observable physical variables. MLPs can approximate these interactions but must learn them implicitly, at a representational cost.

We introduce PRISM (Polynomial Representations for Interaction Structured Motor Control), a physics-motivated yet data-driven representation that learns multiplicative interactions by recursively adding scaled bilinear features, without enumerating all polynomial terms.

Replacing only the MLP's first affine layer, PRISM is plug-and-play for reinforcement and imitation learning, requiring no changes to training objectives, sensing, or controllers. Across humanoid locomotion and contact-rich manipulation, PRISM improves survival from 51.0\% to 92.5\%, outperforming even larger MLPs.

More strikingly, its performance advantage persists under out-of-distribution changes in friction, robot mass, and payload, without retraining.

PRISM also exhibits sensorless compliance-like behavior, increases failure-recovery success from 40.9\% to 52.3\% without explicit admittance control, improves real-robot manipulation, and learns features that better predict physical quantities. These results make PRISM a compelling alternative to standard MLPs for robot policy learning.

The project page is available at https://lsh3163.github.io/prism/.

summary.en: The paper introduces PRISM, a physics-motivated, data-driven representation that learns multiplicative interactions by recursively adding scaled bilinear features, without enumerating all polynomial terms. It replaces only the first affine layer of an MLP policy and requires no changes to training objectives, sensing, or controllers. The authors report humanoid survival rising from 51.0% to 92.5%, with advantages under changes in friction, robot mass, and payload without retraining. They also report improved failure recovery, real-robot manipulation, and features that better predict physical quantities.
summary.zh: 论文提出 PRISM，一种受物理启发、由数据驱动的机器人控制表示，通过递归添加缩放双线性特征来学习物理变量间的乘性交互，而不必枚举全部多项式项。它只替换策略多层感知机的首个仿射层，无需更改训练目标、传感或控制器。作者报告，在人形运动任务中，生存率从51.0%升至92.5%，且在摩擦、机器人质量和负载变化时无需重新训练仍有优势。摘要还报告了无显式导纳控制的恢复成功率提升、真实机器人操作改善及更能预测物理量的特征。

sections.text:
This study introduces TRAIN: TeRrain-Aware Interactive Navigation, a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based framework for quadrupedal navigation across unstructured terrain and human-populated environments. Conventional quadrupedal navigation typically separates motion planning from locomotion control, neglecting whole-body constraints and terrain awareness.

On the other hand, end-to-end methods are more integrated but require high-frequency sensing, which is often noisy and computationally costly. In addition, most existing approaches assume static environments, limiting their use in human-populated settings.

To address these limitations, we propose a two-stage training framework with three DRL pipelines. （1） TRAIN-Loco employs an asymmetric actor-critic (AC) model for quadrupedal locomotion, enabling agile traversal of uneven terrains without explicit terrain or contact observations. （2） TRAIN-Nav applies a symmetric AC framework for navigation with interactive pedestrians, directly mapping transformed LiDAR data to ego-agent actions under differential-drive kinematics. （3） A unified pipeline, TRAIN, integrates TRAIN-Loc and TRAIN-Nav, supporting terrain-aware quadrupedal navigation in uneven and interactive environments.

Comprehensive benchmarks against quadrupedal locomotion and robot navigation baselines demonstrate the effectiveness of TRAIN. Hardware experiments further confirm its potential for sim-to-real transfer.

summary.en: The paper introduces TRAIN, a terrain-aware interactive navigation framework for quadruped robots, trained in two stages through three deep reinforcement learning pipelines. TRAIN-Loco learns locomotion over uneven terrain without explicit terrain or contact observations, while TRAIN-Nav maps transformed LiDAR data to navigation actions around pedestrians. The unified pipeline combines these capabilities. The authors report effective performance in benchmarks against locomotion and navigation baselines, and hardware experiments indicate potential for sim-to-real transfer.
summary.zh: 论文提出 TRAIN，一种面向四足机器人的地形感知交互导航框架，采用两阶段训练和三条深度强化学习流程：TRAIN-Loco 学习不依赖显式地形或接触观测的崎岖地形运动，TRAIN-Nav 将变换后的激光雷达数据映射为与行人交互的导航动作，统一流程则结合两者。作者称基准测试显示该方法有效，硬件实验进一步表明其具有仿真到现实迁移的潜力。

sections.text:
Generative policies can synthesize robot behaviors, yet controlling and editing them through diverse spatiotemporal references remains challenging. In the real world, human intent requires robot behaviors that satisfy constraints on where, when, and how actions are executed.

Our key insight is that spatiotemporal control references, such as keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes, can be viewed as partial specifications of the same temporal Cartesian action space. We introduce the MAP (Masked Action Space) interface to unify these action references and formulate controllable manipulation as an action inpainting problem.

Our Inpainting Policy (IP) reconstructs missing action dimensions of the end-effector, combining progress-guided alignment with multi-mask training to support unseen action-constraint combinations. We further adopt a training-free RePaint variant that iteratively inpaints the action during denoising to reduce control error.

On ManiSkill and LIBERO-10, our policy achieves average task success rates of 92.67% and 64.67%, respectively.Real-world experiments demonstrate spatiotemporal control with average positional and rotational errors of 44.3 mm and 7{\deg}, respectively, showing that our policy can use diverse references to guide executable robot behaviors.

summary.en: The paper introduces the MAP interface, which treats references such as keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes as partial specifications of a temporal Cartesian action space. Its Inpainting Policy reconstructs missing end-effector action dimensions using progress-guided alignment and multi-mask training, while a training-free RePaint variant iteratively inpaints actions during denoising to reduce control error. The authors report average task success rates of 92.67% on ManiSkill and 64.67% on LIBERO-10. Real-world experiments demonstrate spatiotemporal control, with reported positional and rotational errors.
summary.zh: 论文提出 MAP（Masked Action Space）接口，将关键点、流场、方向和关键姿态等时空控制参考统一表示为时间笛卡尔动作空间的部分约束，并将可控操作表述为动作补全问题。其补全策略通过进度引导对齐和多掩码训练重建末端执行器动作，并采用无需训练的 RePaint 变体迭代补全以降低控制误差。作者报告，该方法在 ManiSkill 和 LIBERO-10 上取得相应成功率，并在现实实验中展示时空控制能力及位置、旋转误差。

sections.text:
Refuse collection in pedestrian campuses, parks and mixed-use districts remains manual because compaction trucks cannot reach bins located on walkways, courtyards and building service doors.

This paper presents Mothership, a two-tier autonomous refuse collection system in which an electric compaction truck (the mothership) carries two low-speed sidewalk robots (RoboCarts) that fetch standard two-wheel bins, deliver them to the truck, return the empty bins to their original positions and re-dock on the truck for charging.

The architecture separates responsibilities by scale: the truck performs road driving, compaction, lifting and energy supply, while the carts perform only sidewalk transport and bin grasping.

This split removes the lift-and-tip mechanism from the sidewalk vehicle, keeping it light and low, and relaxes cart-to-truck docking tolerance to the +/-100 mm capture window of a standard automated lifter.

We describe the system architecture, the bin-handling and docking interfaces, and a mission-planning formulation that decomposes a route into truck stop points and cart tasks. A discrete-event simulation over synthetic campus layouts with 2-16 bins/ha quantifies throughput as a function of bin density, cart count and stop-point radius.

A two-cart configuration serves 20-29 bins/h. Throughput is governed by an interaction between cart count and stop-point radius: a single cart performs best with many close stops, whereas three or four carts need wide stops (80 m) to stay busy, reaching 35-49 bins/h at moderate-to-high densities.

The best stop radius therefore has to be chosen together with the fleet size, not fixed in advance.

summary.en: The paper presents Mothership, a two-tier autonomous refuse collection system. An electric compaction truck handles road driving, compaction, lifting, and power, while two low-speed sidewalk robots move standard bins, return emptied bins, and re-dock for charging. The authors describe the interfaces and mission planning, then use discrete-event simulation on synthetic campus layouts. In simulation, a two-cart setup serves 20–29 bins per hour. Throughput depends on coordinating cart count with stop-point radius; more carts can achieve higher throughput with wider stops.

sections.text:
GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra.

We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands.

Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1).

Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control.

We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., {\pi}0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment.

Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks.

We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

summary.en: The report evaluates GPT-6-Astra’s embodied capabilities and their implications. Under a unified protocol allowing in-context learning from training demonstrations and more execution steps, the model achieves what the authors describe as unprecedented performance across 12 benchmarks covering manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. The report also examines high- and low-level control coordination, real-world deployment, and a prototype for future benchmarks. Experiments on eight robot configurations reveal costly demonstration collection and limits on trading longer execution for higher success under physical constraints.
summary.zh: 报告评估 GPT-6-Astra 在具身任务中的能力及其对领域的意义。作者在统一协议下测试 12 个涵盖操作、人形机器人、移动平台和灵巧手的基准，允许从训练示范进行上下文学习并增加执行步数，报告称其表现突出。报告还讨论高低层控制协同、真实部署及下一代基准原型；八种机器人配置的实验显示，示范采集成本高，且受物理约束，延长执行时间难以换取更高成功率。作者认为其已接近具身能力门槛，但尚未达到实用具身智能。

The rise of large language models (LLMs) has opened a path toward generalist embodied AI, raising the question of how LLMs can act in the physical world.

One straightforward approach is training the model to generate actions: collect robot-action data and video demonstration, refine LLM architecture with an action head, and train a vision-language-action (VLA) model at scale. However, we argue that coding agents have the potential to realize generalist embodied manipulation.

All they need is a simple yet effective robot harness. We present RoboHarness: a robotic harness that gives LLM agents a visual-geometric control panel so that they can directly understand and invoke embodied tasks. With RoboHarness, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks. The implementation is open source.

summary.en: The paper presents RoboHarness, a robotic harness that provides LLM agents with a visual-geometric control panel for understanding and invoking embodied tasks. The authors argue that coding agents, given a simple and effective robot harness, can support generalist embodied manipulation. They report that Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with RoboHarness outperforms state-of-the-art VLA models on BEHAVIOR Challenge 2025 tasks. The abstract also states that the implementation is open source.

sections.text:
World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection.

We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress.

Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions.

Within the world-action model, Mixture-of-Transformer Experts integrates modality-specific and shared computation for joint video--action modeling.

Dual-stream hierarchical visual memory maintains temporal context for both models, while subtask-local value learning aligns action evaluation with semantic objectives and preserves supervision from successful prefixes of failed trajectories. LAW achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks.

Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM-$alpha$ further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM also outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High.

On three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for $pi_{0.5}$ and 25% for Fast-WAM.

summary.en: The paper presents LAW, a closed-loop VLM–WAM framework that combines language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Its agent plans remaining subtasks, evaluates and fuses proposed actions, and asynchronously assesses execution. The WAM uses a mixture-of-transformer-experts design for joint video-action modeling; hierarchical visual memory and subtask-local value learning provide additional support. The authors report 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks, 95.56% with an OpenWAM-α backbone, and 65% average success on three long-horizon real-robot tasks.
summary.zh: 论文提出 LAW，一个闭环视觉语言模型与世界动作模型框架，借助语义子任务进度统一语言推理、动作生成和世界建模。智能体规划剩余子任务、评估并融合候选动作，并异步判断执行状态；世界动作模型使用混合专家结构联合建模视频与动作，分层视觉记忆维护时间信息，子任务局部价值学习对齐语义目标。作者报告其在 50 项 RoboTwin 任务上的平均成功率为 94.21%；替换为 OpenWAM-α 后为 95.56%。三项长时程真实机器人任务上的平均成功率为 65%。

items.intro: arXiv:2610.23053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. Large language models (LLMs) enable embodied agents to plan from naturallanguage instructions, yet their actions may be physically infeasible or hazardous. Existing neuro-symbolic learners primarily refine execution models, while formal safety methods acquire or enforce safety constraints.

This separation limits the reuse of both execution corrections and safety knowledge across tasks. We present NEXUS, a modular neuro-symbolic framework that jointly maintains a PDDL domain model and an LTL safety specification.

Execution failures are used to repair action schemas, whereas detected hazards are converted into reusable LTL constraints through hierarchical semantic and translation sampling with equivalence consensus.

Accumulated constraints are enforced through LTL progression during symbolic search; comparing constrained and unconstrained search outcomes distinguishes physical unreachability from safety-induced refusal.

Experiments on SafeAgentBench evaluation set show that NEXUS achieves the best overall trade-off between safetask completion and unsafe-task refusal, while maintaining low violation rates under jailbreak attacks. Ablations confirm the complementary benefits of PDDLdomain refinement and LTL-constraint accumulation.

High-level humanoid planners often output sparse task-space, low-rate trajectories, whereas whole-body controllers run at high frequency. This creates temporal asynchrony between the planning and execution, and structural incompleteness for full-body control. We propose an asynchronous upper body task-space tracking framework for humanoids.

A student policy is initialized by teacher-student distillation, conditioned on the full cached future trajectory and an execution-time index, and trained with a sliding-window global reward to reduce frame drift without explicit frame estimation.

For task-specific post-training, an MPC module completes sparse references into floating-base and upper-body guidance, while action- and FK level self-guidance constrain policy drift.

Simulation and Unitree G1 hardware experiments show improved tracking under low update rates, stronger performance than synchronous and decoupled baselines, and safer adaptation to out-of-distribution motions.

summary.en: This paper presents an asynchronous upper-body task-space tracking framework for humanoid robots, addressing timing differences between low-rate planning and high-frequency whole-body control. A distilled student policy uses cached future trajectories and an execution-time index, with a sliding-window global reward to reduce frame drift. Task-specific post-training uses MPC to complete sparse references and applies action- and forward-kinematics-level self-guidance. Simulation and Unitree G1 hardware experiments show improved low-rate tracking, stronger results than synchronous and decoupled baselines, and safer adaptation to out-of-distribution motions.

sections.text:
To advance the development of embodied intelligence, Open-Environment Active 3D Mapping has attracted increasing attention, aiming to perform a long-horizon and shortest trajectory exploration for reconstructing unseen scenarios.

Since only limited information about unseen environments is available, methods built on the closed-set assumption, i.e., assuming that the test environments are similar to those seen during training, cannot generalize satisfactorily.

In existing active mapping methods, long-horizon exploration is often guided by predicting a coarse long-range goal and then converting it into an executable path. However, this stage is usually formulated as single-point prediction.

Under partial observability, the same local observation may correspond to multiple plausible exploration directions, making such deterministic prediction prone to brittle decisions and degraded performance in unseen scenarios. Our experiments further verify that this is a key factor underlying their weak generalization.

To address this issue, we reformulate long-horizon target prediction as conditional multimodal anchor generation using Conditional Flow Matching. Instead of predicting a single goal, our method learns a conditional distribution over coarse exploration anchors from the current mapping state.

These anchors are first converted into executable candidate paths through obstacle-aware planning. We then apply exploration-mode clustering to compress geometrically similar trajectories and reduce candidate redundancy.

Finally, a hierarchical selection module selects the most promising mode and reranks paths within it to produce the final executable trajectory. Experiments show that our method improves generalization and reconstruction efficiency in open environments.

summary.en: This work addresses generalization in open-environment active 3D mapping, where single-point long-range goal prediction can be brittle under partial observability and multiple plausible exploration directions. It replaces that prediction with conditional multimodal anchor generation using Conditional Flow Matching. Anchors from the current mapping state are converted into obstacle-aware candidate paths, clustered into exploration modes to reduce redundancy, and ranked by a hierarchical selection module. Experiments reported by the authors show improved generalization and reconstruction efficiency in open environments.
summary.zh: 本文关注开放环境主动三维建图中的长时程探索与泛化问题，指出单点远程目标预测在部分可观测条件下容易因多种可能方向而产生脆弱决策。作者将目标预测改为基于条件流匹配的多模态探索锚点生成，从当前建图状态学习锚点分布，再通过避障规划生成候选路径，并以探索模式聚类压缩相似轨迹。分层选择模块先选模式，再对其中路径重排序。实验显示，该方法提升了开放环境中的泛化能力和重建效率。

sections.text:
Reliable 3D person detection is important for rescue robotics to give first responders situational awareness. Yet most multimodal 3D detection research targets automotive scenarios in which pedestrians mostly appear in a narrow range of upright, near-road poses.

It is therefore unclear how much of the reported performance transfers to rescue settings, as a person may be lying, partially occluded, or in unstructured indoor and outdoor environments.

To investigate this gap, we introduce TriSAR-3D, a multimodal person detection dataset recorded with a high-resolution 128-channel LiDAR, an RGB camera, and a thermal camera. It captures varied poses in indoor as well as outdoor locations at different times of day to study their influence on 3D object detector performance.

Furthermore, we propose a novel trimodal 3D detection pipeline, PaintFusion, that fuses PointPainting-based evidence using a simple MLP. We show that the derived method reaches 65.4 AP@50 and thereby outperforms strong LiDAR-only (CenterPoint, 53.4), RGB+LiDAR (BEVFusion, 60.5), and adapted trimodal (Tri-BEVFusion, 60.7) baselines on the dataset.

At the same time, it is substantially faster than other fusion-based methods such as BEVFusion, with a per-frame latency of 51.6 ms compared to 101 ms. Additionally, we test how the performance of different 3D object detectors generalizes to unseen pose categories.

Removing lying instances from training data collapses the lying-pose AP@50 to near zero across all evaluated detectors. The results indicate that dataset diversity exerts a large effect on 3D object detection performance. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/MarkusKramer1/3D-Trimodal-People-Detection.

summary.en: This paper presents TriSAR-3D, a LiDAR, RGB, and thermal dataset for 3D person detection in search-and-rescue settings, and PaintFusion, a trimodal detection pipeline that fuses PointPainting-based evidence with an MLP. The dataset includes varied poses in indoor and outdoor locations. PaintFusion reaches 65.4 AP@50 on the dataset, outperforming the listed LiDAR-only, RGB-plus-LiDAR, and adapted trimodal baselines, with 51.6 ms per-frame latency. Removing lying instances from training brings lying-pose AP@50 near zero across evaluated detectors, indicating the reported influence of dataset diversity.

sections.text:
Echolocating bats navigate dense forests using sonar alone, and in-air 3D imaging sonars now capture the entire frontal hemisphere with every pulse.

Sonar SLAM, however, has so far been planar: current systems estimate a 2D trajectory and discard the elevation information in the sonar images, an assumption that does not hold on rough and sloped terrain such as a forest floor.

In this paper, we introduce RTISSLAM-3D, a novel 6-DoF SLAM system for a wheeled robot that carries an in-air 3D imaging sonar, an IMU and wheel encoders.

A CFAR detector on the sphere reduces every sonar image to a sparse set of 3D detections, which we use for a 3D acoustic odometry that models the shape of the sonar beam, for place recognition with polar submap descriptors, and for the verification of loop closures by 3D registration, all combined in a 6-DoF pose graph with attitude factors.

We evaluated RTISSLAM-3D on a 545m drive through a forest, with a 3D lidar SLAM as reference. The loop closures reduced the horizontal error of the acoustic odometry from 1.74m to 0.28m, with a height error of 0.12m, and 94.6% of the resulting 3D sonar map lies within 0.3 m of the lidar map.

summary.en: The paper presents RTISSLAM-3D, a six-degree-of-freedom SLAM system for a wheeled robot equipped with an in-air 3D imaging sonar, an IMU, and wheel encoders. It converts sonar images into sparse 3D detections for acoustic odometry, place recognition, and loop-closure verification, combining them in a pose graph with attitude factors. In a 545 m forest drive evaluated against 3D lidar SLAM, loop closures reduced horizontal odometry error from 1.74 m to 0.28 m; height error was 0.12 m, and the authors report that 94.6% of the sonar map lies within 0.3 m of the lidar map.

sections.text:
Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require visual information that is no longer present in the current observation. Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory.

We introduce RePlanMem-VLA (Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA), which turns a policy's own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions.

RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event.

We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of 0.981-0.997.

We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100% of episodes.

Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers. Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/.

summary.en: The paper introduces RePlanMem-VLA, which uses large disagreements between overlapping action predictions during receding-horizon execution as signals of task-relevant events. These signals trigger updates to bounded visual memory, while a robot-masked write filter suppresses redundant frames. The authors compare 35 disagreement measures, then validate selected signals on pretrained policies and robot tasks; the detectors achieve ROC-AUC values of 0.981–0.997. In evaluated memory-retention experiments, relevant observations remained available until a later decision point in 100% of episodes. Real-robot replay data also show event selection and redundancy suppression beyond simulation.

sections.text:
General robot skill adaptation requires expressive representations robust to varying task configurations. While recent learning-based skill adaptation methods refined via Reinforcement Learning (RL), have shown success, existing skill models often lack sufficient representational capacity for anything beyond minor environmental changes.

In contrast, Gaussian Process (GP)-based skill modelling provides an expressive representation with useful analytical properties; however, adaptation of GP-based skills remains underexplored. This paper proposes a novel, robust skill adaptation framework that utilises GPs with sparse via-points for compact and expressive modelling.

The model considers the trajectory's poses and leverages its first and second analytical derivatives to preserve the skill's kinematic profile. We present three adaptation methods to cater for the variability between initial and observed configurations.

Firstly, an optimisation agent that adjusts the path's via-points while preserving the demonstration velocity. Second, a behaviour cloning agent trained to replicate output trajectories from the optimisation agent. Lastly, an RL agent that has learnt to modify via-points whilst maintaining the kinematic profile and enabling online capabilities.

Evaluated across three tasks (drawer opening, cube-pushing and bar manipulation) in both simulation and hardware, our proposed methods outperform every benchmark in success rates.

Furthermore, the results demonstrate that the GP-based representation enables all three methods to attain high cosine similarity and low velocity magnitude errors, indicating strong preservation of the kinematic profile. Overall, our formulation provides a compact representation capable of adapting to large deviations from a single demonstrated skill.

summary.en: The paper proposes a Gaussian-process-based framework for adapting robot skills, using sparse via-points to represent trajectory poses and analytical first and second derivatives to preserve kinematic profiles. It presents three adaptation methods: an optimizer that adjusts via-points while preserving demonstrated velocity, a behavior-cloning agent that imitates the optimizer's trajectories, and an RL agent that modifies via-points online while maintaining the profile. In simulation and hardware evaluations across drawer opening, cube pushing, and bar manipulation, the authors report higher success rates than all benchmarks. Results also show high cosine similarity and low velocity-magnitude errors.
