sections.text:
Due to the high cost of hardware experiments, robot policies are predominantly evaluated by comparing their empirical performance on a limited number of hardware trials. However, finite-sample statistical uncertainty can lead to erroneous conclusions, especially when ranking multiple policies using a fixed batch of evaluation data.

We propose AnyRank: a sequential method for multi-policy ranking that (i) adaptively allocates trials to hard-to-separate policies, (ii) provides (partial) rankings at any stopping time while bounding the probability of an incorrect ranking, and (iii) optionally exploits prior information to prioritize hardware evaluations more efficiently.

This prior information could be informed from expert intuition, a small set of held-out hardware evaluations, or from policy rollouts in a simulator or an action-conditioned video world model.

Notably, the prior can be imperfect; while a strong prior can provide efficiency gains on hardware, any inaccuracies in prior policy rankings do not invalidate the statistical assurances of AnyRank.

We achieve the aforementioned properties through novel theoretical contributions that combine sequential testing with multiple-hypothesis graphical testing approaches.

Experiments in simulation and real-world policy evaluation benchmarks show that AnyRank requires up to 50% fewer hardware evaluations compared to existing statistically rigorous approaches, while guarding against the incorrect rankings produced by heuristic methods used by state-of-the-art benchmarks.

summary.en: The paper proposes AnyRank, a sequential method for ranking multiple robot policies. It adaptively allocates trials to policies that are difficult to distinguish, provides partial or complete rankings at any stopping time with a bound on the probability of error, and can use potentially imperfect prior information to prioritize hardware evaluations without invalidating its statistical guarantees. The method combines sequential testing with graphical multiple-hypothesis testing. Simulation and real-world benchmark experiments report up to 50% fewer hardware evaluations than existing statistically rigorous approaches.
summary.zh: 论文提出 AnyRank，一种用于多策略排序的序贯方法。它会把试验自适应分配给难以区分的策略，可在任意停止时刻给出部分或完整排序，并控制排序错误概率；也可利用可能不完美的先验信息安排硬件评估，先验排序不准确不会破坏其统计保证。方法结合序贯检验与多重假设图检验。仿真和真实世界策略评估基准实验显示，相比现有严谨统计方法，AnyRank 最多可减少 50% 的硬件评估，并防范启发式方法产生的错误排序。

sections.text:
Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement.

We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs.

In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance.

Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop.

Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales.

In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions.

The authors report a 37.4% average advantage over top baselines in simulation and continued improvement on real-robot tasks without human demonstrations.

sections.text:
World models provide robots with a predictive mechanism for reasoning about how actions change object states in manipulation tasks.

However, existing image-based and dense 3D world models do not explicitly impose object-level rigid motion, leaving rigid-object geometry preservation to be learned implicitly and making multi-step rollouts susceptible to shape drift or object-level motion inconsistency.

To address this, we propose ORD-WM, a 3D world model that learns object-centric rigid dynamics for robotic manipulation.

ORD-WM learns a vector-neuron variational autoencoder supervised by signed distance fields, which encodes each object point cloud as a geometry-aware latent representation composed of 3D vector features, and uses an action-conditioned dynamics model to predict object-wise SE（3） motion increments.

Rather than generating unconstrained next latent states, ORD-WM analytically applies predicted object-wise rigid transformations to the current latent states, separating persistent object geometry from pose changes.

Experiments show that ORD-WM enables stable, geometry-preserving multi-step prediction and supports efficient real-time replanning for closed-loop model predictive control in simulated and real-world manipulation scenarios.

summary.en: The paper presents ORD-WM, a 3D world model for robotic manipulation that explicitly learns object-centric rigid dynamics. A signed-distance-field-supervised vector-neuron variational autoencoder represents object point clouds, while an action-conditioned model predicts object-wise SE(3) motion increments. ORD-WM analytically applies these rigid transformations to current latent states, separating persistent geometry from pose changes. Experiments show stable multi-step predictions that preserve geometry and support efficient real-time replanning for closed-loop model predictive control in simulated and real-world manipulation scenarios.

sections.text:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly regress joint-space actions avoid the deployment-time cost of inverse kinematics.

However, their training objectives remain misaligned with task success, as joint-space losses ignore the unequal physical consequences of joint errors and visual conditioning lacks explicit focus on hand-object interaction regions. To address these issues, we propose a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation.

First, a physics-grounded flow-matching loss maps the implicit clean-action estimate at every noise level through differentiable forward kinematics (FK) and supervises the resulting Tool Center Point (TCP) pose and inter-arm relative pose, with a bounded noise-level weighting that compensates gradient decay.

Second, we introduce a global prediction query group distilled from a frozen DINOv3 teacher through future-frame feature prediction, together with a local interaction query supervised by Grounding DINO at the attention level.

Both teachers are removed at inference, and the deployment pipeline is that of a standard joint-space flow policy, adding only the learned query pathway. Simulation and real-robot experiments on long-horizon bimanual tasks show that the two priors are complementary across different deployment settings.

The full model excels in in-distribution deployment, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.

summary.en: The paper proposes GRASP, a training-phase prior-injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation, addressing gaps between joint-space training losses and task success. Its physics-grounded flow-matching loss uses differentiable forward kinematics to supervise tool-center-point and inter-arm poses. A global prediction query is distilled from a frozen DINOv3 teacher, while Grounding DINO supervises a local interaction query. Teachers are removed at inference, leaving a standard joint-space flow policy with a learned query pathway. Simulation and real-robot experiments report complementary benefits: the full model excels in-distribution, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.

sections.text:
Space robots must interpret tasks and act despite unfamiliar dynamics, difficult sensing conditions, and limited opportunities for human intervention. Foundation models offer reusable perceptual and behavioral knowledge, but their value depends on how that knowledge reaches physical execution.

This critical review follows space-specific requirements through perception, prediction, planning, and action to deployment and validation, emphasizing orbital manipulation and proximity operations.

Terrestrial comparisons establish benefits of particular pretraining stages and model interfaces; their transfer to space dynamics and constrained onboard operation remains insufficiently tested.

Event cameras offer timely motion observations across strong illumination contrasts, while spiking neural networks provide possible routes to sparse local computation. We examine how sensor degradation, state estimation and computing choices affect feedback and recovery.

Higher action throughput need not yield fresher feedback; lower processor power can also coexist with higher energy per inference. We organize validation as an iterative sim-to-ground-to-space pathway, connecting physical tests with telemetry-based diagnosis and closed-loop revalidation.

A satellite-capture example links observations to approach, contact and recovery, while a corresponding protocol separates generalization from adaptation with limited target-domain interaction. These comparisons identify what models already contribute and the physical evidence needed to support autonomous space operation.

summary.en: This critical review examines foundation models for autonomous space robotics, focusing on perception, prediction, planning, action, deployment, and validation in orbital manipulation and proximity operations. The authors say transfer from terrestrial pretraining and model interfaces to space dynamics and constrained onboard computing remains insufficiently tested. They discuss event cameras, spiking neural networks, sensing degradation, state estimation, and feedback, and organize validation as an iterative sim-to-ground-to-space pathway. A satellite-capture example and protocol distinguish generalization from adaptation with limited target-domain interaction.
summary.zh: 本文综述基础模型用于自主空间机器人的要求、架构与验证，重点讨论轨道操作和近距离运行中的感知、预测、规划、动作及部署。作者指出，陆地预训练和模型接口的优势能否迁移到空间动力学及受限星载计算，仍缺乏充分测试。文章考察事件相机、脉冲神经网络、传感器退化、状态估计和算力选择对反馈与恢复的影响，并提出从仿真到地面再到空间的迭代验证路径。卫星捕获示例及协议用于区分泛化与有限目标域交互下的适应。

sections.text:
Autonomously navigating off-road terrain at high speed demands accurate control, which often relies on dynamics models that capture complex interactions between the robot and terrain. In off-road regimes, terrain interaction is a major component of the vehicle's dynamics.

Prior work attempts to capture this effect by training learned models of the vehicle's dynamics, conditioned on its perception of the local environment. However, said conditioning is often overly simplistic, ignoring the spatial structure of the dynamics problem. Our approach, SpatialBEV, exploits this spatial structure.

At each step, we query the bird's-eye-view (BEV) features around the predicted state, conditioning the next prediction on current geometric and semantic cues. We additionally present a benchmarking approach that mines a dataset's most difficult scenarios.

On datasets collected across seasons, SpatialBEV reduces prediction error by 17.1%, compared to physics-based and learned baselines. We further evaluate on hardware on high-speed ($\geq$10 m/s) and geometrically challenging courses with a 25.3% reduction in maximum cross-track error. More details can be found at https://theairlab.org/spatial-bev-dynamics .

summary.en: SpatialBEV addresses limited spatial structure in learned off-road vehicle dynamics by querying bird’s-eye-view features around the predicted state at each step and conditioning the next prediction on geometric and semantic cues. The authors also propose a benchmark approach that mines difficult dataset scenarios. Across datasets collected in different seasons, SpatialBEV reduces prediction error by 17.1% relative to physics-based and learned baselines. In hardware evaluations on high-speed, geometrically challenging courses, it reduces maximum cross-track error by 25.3%.
summary.zh: SpatialBEV针对越野车辆动力学学习中对局部环境空间结构刻画不足的问题，在每一步根据预测状态查询鸟瞰图特征，并以几何和语义线索条件化下一步预测。作者还提出一种挖掘数据集中困难场景的基准测试方法。在跨季节采集的数据集上，该方法相较物理模型和学习基线将预测误差降低17.1%；硬件评估中，在高速且几何复杂的赛道上，最大横向轨迹误差降低25.3%。这些结果分别来自数据集评估和硬件测试。

sections.text:
Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for.

Adapting them to a new experiment still takes extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal.

SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together.

We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting the role of human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable.

Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

summary.en: The paper introduces the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates a laboratory setup from a high-level scientific goal. Starting with anything from an empty room to an existing self-driving lab, it builds missing capabilities such as layout, a digital twin, robot skills, and workflows. The authors demonstrate SBL across different robots and setups, from one workstation to laboratories with multiple collaborating robots. They validate its end-to-end capabilities in a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment, with researchers specifying objectives.

sections.text:
Tactile sensing can improve performance in contact-rich robot manipulation. However, learning policies that use real tactile feedback typically requires demonstrations collected with tactile-equipped hardware.

We present Feature-Extracted Latent Tactile (FELT), a framework that uses existing paired visuo-tactile data to learn contact-aware representations from RGB observations. FELT provides these representations to downstream policies through two interfaces: generated tactile images and contact-aware features.

FELT combines a frozen visual encoder with separate query decoders for the left and right finger, reflecting the spatial organization of dual-finger tactile arrays. The two branches exchange information through gated connections, and a convolutional readout produces spatial contact representations for the downstream interfaces.

For downstream manipulation, the image interface decodes these spatial representations into tactile images, allowing policies trained with either real or generated tactile observations to use generated images at deployment.

Alternatively, the feature interface feeds these representations directly to the policy during both training and deployment, without real tactile observations. Experiments on four contact-rich real-robot tasks show that both interfaces achieve higher success rates than vision-only policies.

Directly incorporating learned contact-aware features into the policy improves success by 15-22.5 percentage points across the four tasks.

summary.en: FELT learns contact-aware representations from RGB observations using existing paired visuo-tactile data, then provides them to manipulation policies as generated tactile images or direct features. Its architecture uses a frozen visual encoder, separate query decoders for the two fingers, and gated connections. The image interface lets policies use generated tactile images at deployment; the feature interface supplies representations during both training and deployment without real tactile observations. In experiments on four real-robot contact-rich tasks, both interfaces outperform vision-only policies, while the feature interface improves success by 15–22.5 percentage points.

sections.text:
Contact locations and interaction forces are critical for contact-rich robot manipulation but are often ambiguous from vision alone. Measuring them on robots requires specialized tactile hardware and platform-specific data collection, which keeps robot tactile data scarce. Human egocentric video is far easier to scale but lacks touch.

Recent predictors trained on egocentric recordings paired with tactile-glove measurements can predict this missing signal from video alone. These predictors, however, remain confined to human hands, which differ from robot hands in appearance and tactile layout.

We present Ego2Contact, which learns a visual-tactile prior from human interactions and transfers it to robot hands. Its predictor fuses temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to infer bimanual tactile fields from the RGB video.

Anatomical region correspondences align varying robot tactile layouts with the predictor's canonical grid, turning robot measurements into fine-tuning targets and predictions into policy inputs. Ego2Contact outperforms prior tactile predictors on human data, including unseen objects, and on robot data after adaptation.

The adapted predictor provides tactile inputs for both simulated reinforcement learning and real-robot policy post-training. In simulation, policies using predicted touch outperform non-tactile baselines and recover part of the benefit of ground-truth tactile sensing.

These results show that human-learned tactile priors can supply touch when direct tactile sensing is limited.

summary.en: Ego2Contact learns a visual-tactile prior from human egocentric interactions and transfers it to robot hands. It combines temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to predict bimanual tactile fields from RGB video, using anatomical correspondences to align different robot sensor layouts and robot measurements for fine-tuning. The authors report better performance than prior predictors on human data and adapted robot data. In simulation, policies using predicted touch outperform non-tactile baselines and recover part of the benefit of ground-truth touch; the predictor is also used for real-robot policy post-training.

sections.text:
Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures.

As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly capable, an important question remains: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? We present SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework developed through studies of navigation formulation, data construction, and optimization.

At the formulation level, SimpleVLN combines single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global-local memory to efficiently use navigation history without unbounded context growth, while action chunks enable efficient output of multiple primitive actions per model invocation.

For data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent DAgger experience and develop a scalable synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale tasks for reinforcement learning. At the optimization level, a progressive IL-DAgger-RL pipeline advances from action imitation to task-level outcome optimization.

Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7% and 80.1% success rates on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods.

These results show that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.

summary.en: SimpleVLN is a vision-language navigation framework that preserves native multimodal language model architectures. Its design combines single-turn decisions, fixed-budget global-local memory, and action chunks with expert demonstrations, policy-dependent DAgger experience, and synthesized tasks. Training progresses from imitation learning through DAgger to reinforcement learning focused on task outcomes. The authors report that it generalizes across multiple model backbones and sizes, achieving success rates of 76.7% on R2R-CE and 80.1% on RxR-CE, outperforming existing methods on those splits.

Enabling embodied agents to imagine future states is essential for robust and generalizable visual navigation. Yet, state-of-the-art systems typically rely on modular designs that decouple navigation planning from visual world modeling, which often induces state-action misalignment and weak adaptability in novel or dynamic scenarios.

We propose UniWM, a unified, memory-augmented world model that integrates egocentric visual foresight and planning within a single multimodal autoregressive backbone. UniWM explicitly grounds action selection in visually imagined outcomes, tightly aligning prediction with control.

Meanwhile, a hierarchical memory mechanism fuses short-term perceptual cues with longer-term trajectory context, supporting stable and coherent reasoning over extended horizons.

Extensive experiments on four challenging benchmarks (Go Stanford, ReCon, SCAND, HuRoN) and the 1X Humanoid Dataset show that UniWM improves navigation success rates by up to 30%, substantially reduces trajectory errors against strong baselines, generalizes zero-shot to the unseen TartanDrive dataset, and scales naturally to high-dimensional humanoid navigation.

These results position UniWM as a principled step toward unified, imagination-driven embodied navigation. The code and models are available at https://github.com/UWMILab/UniWM.

summary.en: UniWM is a unified, memory-augmented world model that integrates egocentric visual foresight and navigation planning in one multimodal autoregressive backbone. It grounds action choices in imagined visual outcomes and combines short-term perceptual cues with longer-term trajectory context. Across four benchmarks and the 1X Humanoid Dataset, the authors report navigation success improvements of up to 30%, reduced trajectory errors against strong baselines, zero-shot generalization to the unseen TartanDrive dataset, and scaling to high-dimensional humanoid navigation.
summary.zh: 论文提出 UniWM，将第一人称视觉预见与导航规划整合进单一多模态自回归世界模型，使动作选择依据想象的视觉结果。其分层记忆结合短期感知线索和长期轨迹信息，以支持长时程推理。作者在四个基准和 1X Humanoid Dataset 上报告，UniWM 的导航成功率最高提升 30%，相较强基线减少轨迹误差，并能零样本泛化至未见的 TartanDrive 数据集；论文还称其可扩展至高维人形机器人导航。

Achieving precise terminal position and heading alignment remains a significant challenge for learning-based mobile robot control.

Recent vision-based learning methods have shown promise for precise target-relative control and generalization to unseen environments with pretrained visual encoders, but general-purpose visual representations are not specifically designed to capture the fine-grained spatial differences between current and goal views required for precise control, and real-world demonstrations combining millimeter-scale terminal accuracy with zero-shot transfer across environments remain limited.

To address these challenges, we propose Geometric Representation Conditioning for Precise Visuomotor Policy (GR-VIP), a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy that leverages a visual encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation.

Rather than using the final relative-pose estimate, GR-VIP conditions action prediction on the dense relational features produced before pose regression, preserving fine-grained cross-view information for learning corrective actions from demonstrations.

We evaluate GR-VIP on a real-world docking task and demonstrate high docking success rates and millimeter-scale terminal accuracy in both the training and unseen environments, without additional training for transfer.

Furthermore, supplementary experiments illustrate the policy's ability to align with non-docking targets and complete docking under a tested low-light condition.

summary.en: The paper proposes GR-VIP, a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy intended to improve terminal position and heading alignment for mobile robots. It uses a visual encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation and conditions action prediction on dense relational features produced before pose regression, learning corrective actions from demonstrations. The authors report high success rates and millimeter-scale terminal accuracy on a real-world docking task in both training and unseen environments, without additional transfer training. Supplementary experiments show alignment with non-docking targets and docking under a tested low-light condition.

sections.text:
Sequential robot manipulation requires policies to execute novel combinations of familiar instruction components. However, collecting demonstrations for all possible instruction tuples is combinatorially expensive, while sparsely covered datasets often fail under out-of-distribution recombination.

This paper studies compositional generalization through the lens of instruction-space coverage. We decompose the generalization gap into three sources: \textit{marginal instruction shift}, \textit{instruction-compositional shift}, and \textit{context--action shift}.

This decomposition allows us to diagnose when sparse training coverage is sufficient, and what structure the training set must preserve for reliable action prediction. Our results show that exhaustive tuple enumeration is unnecessary: a structured subset can recover strong out-of-distribution performance when it covers action-relevant dependencies.

We further find that sparse training often fails due to instruction steering rather than missing low-level skills; finetuning with only one demonstration per task improves OOD success from \(0.4\%\) to \(54.7\%\).For semantically dependent tasks, effective coverage must capture relational structure rather than only factor diversity.

These findings suggest that efficient robot data collection should prioritize dependency coverage in instruction space over exhaustive task expansion. Additional results, code, and dataset are available on the \href{https://yixiaowang7.github.io/Diagnosing_Compositional_Generalization_Robot_Page/}{project website}.

summary.en: The paper studies compositional generalization in sequential robot manipulation and decomposes the generalization gap into marginal instruction shift, instruction-compositional shift, and context-action shift. The authors argue that exhaustive enumeration of instruction tuples is unnecessary: a structured training subset can yield strong out-of-distribution performance when it covers action-relevant dependencies. They also report that sparse training often fails through instruction steering, and that fine-tuning with one demonstration per task raises OOD success from 0.4% to 54.7%. Semantically dependent tasks require coverage of relational structure.

We use a frozen frontier vision-language model, GPT-6-Astra, directly as the robot policy on RoboMME, a benchmark of 16 memory-dependent manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory. The model keeps the whole episode in context and outputs every end-effector waypoint and gripper command, with no RoboMME-specific training.

On the 800 test episodes it succeeds in 92.1%, above the previously reported human score of 90.5%, which was obtained with an oracle skill interface, and far ahead of the best leaderboard entry (60.8%) and of a hierarchical system that pairs the same model with a RoboMME-trained policy (79.1%).It matches or exceeds the human score on 13 of the 16 tasks.

Its 63 failures concentrate in two tasks and are mostly premature completions and mistimed or unintended button presses. These results blur the usual division between long-horizon planning, memory and end-effector control, and raise the question of how much of this stack a single general-purpose model can take over in embodied systems.

Project website: https://embodied-astra.github.io. Code, prompts and all episode logs: https://github.com/jackbjed/embodied-astra-robomme.

summary.en: The paper evaluates a frozen frontier vision-language model as a robot policy on RoboMME’s 16 memory-dependent manipulation tasks, without benchmark-specific training. The model retains the episode context and outputs end-effector waypoints and gripper commands. The authors report a 92.1% success rate over 800 test episodes, above a previously reported 90.5% human score obtained with an oracle skill interface. The model matches or exceeds that human score on 13 tasks; its failures are concentrated in two tasks.

sections.text:
Dense visual odometry (VO), which provides pose estimation and dense 3D reconstruction, serves as the cornerstone for applications ranging from robotics to augmented reality. Recently, feed-forward models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in dense mapping.

However, when these models are used in dense visual SLAM systems, their keyframe-based processing often leads to sparse pose outputs, limiting continuous per-frame pose estimation. In contrast, traditional sparse methods provide high-frequency pose outputs but lack the capability for dense reconstruction.

To address these limitations, we propose HyVGGT-VO, a novel framework that combines the computational efficiency of sparse VO with the dense reconstruction capabilities of feed-forward model. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to tightly couple a traditional VO frontend with VGGT.

Specifically, we design an adaptive hybrid tracking frontend that dynamically switches between traditional optical flow and the VGGT model to ensure robustness. Furthermore, we introduce a hierarchical optimization framework that jointly refines VO poses and the scale of VGGT predictions to ensure global scale consistency.

Under the odometry setting, compared with VGGT-SLAM 2.0, HyVGGT-VO reduces the average ATE by approximately 91% on EuRoC MAV and 20% on TUM RGB-D, and decreases the average relative translation and rotation errors by 46% and 92% on KITTI, respectively, while achieving 16.1 Hz pose output and 3.2 Hz dense-mapping updates with 6.5 GB of memory on an 8 GB laptop GPU.Our code is available at https://geneta2580.github.io/HyVGGT-VO.io.

summary.en: The paper presents HyVGGT-VO, combining sparse traditional visual odometry with the VGGT feed-forward model for frequent pose estimates and dense reconstruction. Its adaptive tracking frontend switches between optical flow and VGGT, while hierarchical optimization jointly refines poses and prediction scale. In odometry evaluations on EuRoC MAV, TUM RGB-D, and KITTI, the authors report lower error measures than VGGT-SLAM 2.0. They also report pose and mapping update rates and memory use on an 8 GB laptop GPU.

sections.text:
Robots manipulating objects in clutter must decide not only how to act, but also where to look. Although active camera motion can expose an occluded target, it may move the robot into an initial observation-state distribution that differs from the manipulation policy's training distribution.

We identify this problem as first-frame distribution sensitivity: under perturbed starts in LIBERO, naively prepending camera repositioning to pi_0.5 reduces success from 46.3% to 11.5%.We introduce ActiveAlign, a data-adaptation framework that trains a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy from the states at which active perception terminates.

A learned viewpoint module first generates a camera trajectory. Offline, ActiveAlign uses closed-loop alignment to connect the trajectory endpoint to an existing demonstration, replays the remaining manipulation trajectory, and retains successful continuations for fine-tuning.

At deployment, the same viewpoint module precedes the adapted VLA without modifying its architecture. Across 40 LIBERO tasks, ActiveAlign achieves 70.7% success with pi_0 and 72.7% with pi_0.5, outperforming their standard-training baselines by 40.0% and 26.4% respectively.

Matched-state and data-matched controls support gains beyond prefix shortening and generic viewpoint augmentation; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 also show the same trend. Success rate under physical occlusion in real world increases from 35/90 to 83/90.

These results show that active perception benefits manipulation when policy training is aligned with the observation and robot-state distribution induced by viewpoint selection.

summary.en: The paper introduces ActiveAlign to address a mismatch between the initial observations induced by active camera movement and a manipulation policy's training distribution. Offline, it connects viewpoint trajectory endpoints to demonstrations, replays subsequent actions, and fine-tunes a vision-language-action policy on successful continuations. At deployment, the viewpoint module precedes the unchanged policy. The authors report higher success than standard-training baselines across 40 LIBERO tasks, a similar trend for OpenVLA and GR00T N1, and more successes under physical occlusion in the real world.
summary.zh: 论文提出 ActiveAlign，针对主动调整摄像头视角后，机器人初始观测状态与操作策略训练分布不一致的问题。该方法离线连接视角轨迹终点与已有示范，回放操作后续轨迹，并用成功片段微调视觉语言动作策略；部署时先运行视角模块，不改策略架构。作者报告，在 40 项 LIBERO 任务中，策略成功率超过标准训练基线，且 OpenVLA、GR00T N1 呈现相同趋势；真实世界物理遮挡条件下的成功次数也有所增加。

sections.text:
Robotic vacuum cleaners must extend their functionality within tight limits on size, cost, and durability. Deployable linkages with few actuators meet these limits, but their backdrivability makes it difficult to hold a load-bearing posture without continuous motor torque. We introduce a two-stage deployable linkage that locks through its own geometry.

At full deployment, an internal three-link subchain approaches a collinear, near-singular configuration in which the input-output transmission ratio tends to zero; plate loads therefore leave only a small residual back-driving torque, which drive-train friction and a lightweight magnetic detent absorb.

A single actuator performs deployment and locking, a passive chassis-mounted trigger releases the lock for retraction, and a second actuator adjusts only the deployment height.

We integrate the mechanism into a commercial robotic vacuum cleaner and validate it through a 100-cycle repeatability test, a quasi-static load test in which the locked plate held 50 N with the motor de-energized, and 140 pushing-type tidying trials on seven household objects against a commercial arm-equipped vacuum robot.

We derive the analytical holding condition and discuss its limits as an intermediate design point between passive compliance and articulated manipulation.

Massive robot swarms can explore unknown environments quickly, but adding robots eventually stops helping. Doorways and dense traffic create congestion, increasing inter-robot contacts and reducing the value of each additional robot. We study this safety-efficiency tradeoff for ground swarms of tens to hundreds of robots.

We present SPACE, Swarm Pheromone Fields for Adaptive Collision-Aware Exploration. Inspired by ant foraging, SPACE maintains a shared environmental field with an attractive frontier pheromone, a repellent explore pheromone, and a fast robot-density field. Robots use local field guidance on a synchronized shared map.

We evaluate SPACE on real building floorplans, namely sixteen home layouts from the HouseExpo dataset and eight campus floors from the KTH dataset, with swarms of up to two hundred and fifty-six robots.

At congested swarm sizes, SPACE attains the lowest inter-robot contact rate on HouseExpo and lies on the empirical Pareto frontier on KTH, together with handed lane formation at sizes where Lane has fewer contacts.

Relative to a greedy nearest-frontier planner, SPACE reduces the contact rate by four to seventeen times while keeping coverage time within about two percent. The results indicate that, at this scale, coordination mainly improves safety rather than coverage time.

sections.text:
This study presents an interdisciplinary process for benchmarking service robots in public everyday environments, addressing the gap between laboratory metrics and real-world operation at technology readiness levels 6-7.

Three robots were evaluated in three use cases: outdoor park cleaning, pedestrian underpass cleaning, and interactive assistance in a public library.

Over three years (2023-2025), seven benchmarking events (a consensus workshop and six on-site evaluations, two per use case) assessed the robots in increasingly realistic settings, from controlled conditions to public operation.

An interdisciplinary panel of experts in robotics, human-robot interaction, safety, and economic viability consolidated use-case-specific metrics into a shared evaluation concept refined across three phases.

Rather than ranking the robots, the evaluation examined how task fulfillment, interaction quality, safety, and economic viability interact in the transition from laboratory prototype to operational system. Direct quantitative comparability across the heterogeneous use cases remained limited, characteristic of benchmarking at this maturity level.

The process yielded cross-case insights: increasing environmental realism introduces challenges that uniform metrics capture only in part; the interaction-quality guideline works best as a modular instrument adapted to each use case; safety was assessed by occupational-safety and product-certification experts who adapted industrial test procedures for public settings; and economic viability proved a cross-cutting dimension.

We conclude that benchmarking at higher technology readiness levels is well served by a shared procedure for selecting and documenting metrics across these four categories, with safety as mandatory, rather than by a fixed set of metrics: generalizability lies in the procedure rather than in identical metrics.

items.title: Benchmarking Robots for Everyday Environments: From Lab Experiments to Real-World Operations

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are rapidly expanding what individual robots can accomplish, yet many real-world manipulation settings require multiple arms to operate as a coordinated system.

Existing approaches organize multi-arm coordination in different ways, including centralized joint policies, high-level task or role assignment, and locally executed policies that react to teammates. However, how complete action-producing VLAs should explicitly interact with one another during action generation remains largely unexplored.

We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes one complete VLA per arm while preserving local perception and action ownership, and enables coordination through learned interaction across policy boundaries.

We first systematically study where such interaction should occur, how peer information should be aggregated, and how the interaction should be learned, revealing complementary coordination functions spanning shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction.

We then re-instantiate these functions in a structurally different VLA architecture, showing that the coordination principle is not tied to a particular tensor layout or backbone implementation. Finally, we compose teams of three and four arms and evaluate them in simulation and physical experiments.

On all four physical tasks, Full interaction improves success over independently trained local policies by 16--40 percentage points. Together, these results suggest that explicit interaction among complete VLA policies offers a scalable path toward networked embodied intelligence.

summary.en: The paper presents VLA-Fabric, assigning a complete vision-language-action policy to each arm while retaining local perception and action ownership. Learned interactions across policies support coordination. The authors study where interaction occurs, how peer information is aggregated, and how it is learned, identifying complementary functions involving shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction. They reinstantiate the approach in a different VLA architecture. In simulation and physical experiments with three- and four-arm teams, full interaction improves success by 16–40 percentage points over independently trained local policies on four physical tasks.

sections.text:
Dexterous grasp synthesis has advanced rapidly in generating stable and physically plausible hand poses, but real-world manipulation requires grasps that preserve the function implied by the task.

We study open-vocabulary task-oriented dexterous grasp generation, where a robot must infer functional intent from free-form language, ground it in multi-view visual observations and object geometry, and generate an executable high-degree-of-freedom grasp. We present OpenDexGrasp, a unified data and generative modeling framework for this setting.

OpenDexVerse provides dual-source supervision organized by the Coverage-to-Alignment (C2A) Recipe: OpenDex-Scale offers large-scale semantic and geometric coverage through automatic grasp synthesis and vision-language annotation, while OpenDex-Align supplies high-quality embodied alignment through human teleoperation and category-level transfer.

OpenDexGrasp learns a shared perception-action latent representation that couples open-vocabulary vision-language context with dexterous action generation.

Affordance grounding and grasp generation provide complementary supervision over this latent space, enabling direct generation of task-consistent dexterous grasps without a separate affordance-to-pose inference stage.

Extensive simulation and real-robot experiments demonstrate improved functional alignment, physical feasibility, generalization to unseen categories, and real-world execution success. Additional details and videos are available at https://opendexgrasp.github.io/.

summary.en: The paper studies open-vocabulary, task-oriented dexterous grasp generation: a robot infers functional intent from free-form language, grounds it in multi-view observations and object geometry, and generates an executable high-degree-of-freedom grasp. OpenDexGrasp combines a data and generative modeling framework with OpenDexVerse, whose C2A recipe pairs broad semantic and geometric coverage from automatic synthesis and vision-language annotation with embodied alignment from human teleoperation and category-level transfer. A shared perception-action latent representation is supervised by affordance grounding and grasp generation. The authors report improvements in functional alignment, physical feasibility, unseen-category generalization, and real-robot execution across simulation and real-robot experiments.
summary.zh: 本文研究开放词汇、面向任务的灵巧抓取：机器人需从自由形式语言推断功能意图，结合多视角观察和物体几何，生成可执行的高自由度抓取。OpenDexGrasp 是统一的数据与生成建模框架，其 OpenDexVerse 按 C2A 方案结合自动抓取合成与视觉语言标注形成的规模化语义和几何覆盖，以及人工遥操作和类别迁移形成的具身对齐数据。模型学习共享感知—动作潜在表示，以功能可供性定位和抓取生成共同监督，直接生成符合任务的抓取。作者报告，仿真及真实机器人实验显示其功能对齐、物理可行性、未见类别泛化和实际执行成功表现有所改善。

items.title: OpenDexGrasp: Open-vocabulary Task-Oriented Dexterous Grasping

Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable.

Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences. We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation.

Its vision-action-force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies.

To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution.

Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively.

Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy. These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.

Its vision-action-force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts visual and force responses to planned actions; a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending deviations. The authors also introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset with 2,852 trajectories across 18 tasks and frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution. Experiments on seen and novel tasks report more accurate discrimination and earlier warnings than representative baselines. Using predictions for anomaly-aware action selection raises end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5%, without retraining the underlying manipulation policy.

sections.text:
Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs), such as wires and cables, are central to industrial assembly.

Unlike rigid objects, whose state is captured by a 6-DoF pose, DLOs have an infinite-dimensional configuration space and deform continuously under contact with grippers, fixtures, and the workspace, making them a demanding benchmark for general dexterous manipulation.

Despite their importance, policy development and comparison remain difficult: existing benchmarks are often tied to specific hardware setups, lack modular and customizable task assets, or study generic deformable-object tasks without the fixtures relevant to real-world industrial wire manipulation.

Few benchmarks align simulation, real-world data, and shared evaluation protocols. To bridge this gap, we introduce WireCraft, a simulation benchmark for industrial DLO manipulation with configurable difficulty and assets, spanning three task families: connector insertion, clip routing, and channel seating.

It supports two complementary DLO physics models, articulated and deformable, and the released trajectories come from both simulation and a physical UR5.We benchmark reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning (IL), and vision-language-action (VLA) policies under shared metrics.

Privileged state-based RL solves a representative setting in each task family with over 82% success, confirming the tasks are well-posed. Image-based policies remain less successful across the evaluated tasks, with ACT and DiT VLA falling below privileged State PPO.

On a physical UR5, supplementing real demonstrations with simulated data improves success by 15-65 percentage points in the best-performing mixture for each task. These results indicate that industrial DLO manipulation, though tractable under privileged state, remains an open challenge for current vision-based learning.

summary.en: The paper presents WireCraft, a simulation benchmark for industrial deformable linear object (DLO) manipulation. It covers connector insertion, clip routing, and channel seating, with configurable difficulty and assets and two physics models: articulated and deformable. The benchmark includes simulation and physical UR5 trajectories and compares reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and vision-language-action policies using shared metrics. The authors report that privileged state-based RL exceeds 82% success in representative settings across the task families, while image-based policies perform less well. On a physical UR5, adding simulated data to real demonstrations improves success by 15–65 percentage points in the best-performing mixture for each task.
summary.zh: 本文介绍 WireCraft，一个面向工业线缆等可变形线状物体（DLO）操作的仿真基准，包含连接器插入、卡扣布线和通道入线三类任务，并支持可配置难度、任务资产及关节式和可变形式两种物理模型。基准提供仿真与实体 UR5 轨迹，并以共享指标比较强化学习、模仿学习和视觉—语言—动作策略。作者报告，特权状态强化学习在各任务族的代表性设置中成功率超过 82%；图像策略表现较低。实体 UR5 实验中，为真实示范补充仿真数据，在各任务最佳数据混合下使成功率提高 15–65 个百分点。作者据此指出，工业 DLO 操作对当前视觉学习仍具挑战。

sections.text:
Long-horizon robotic tasks expose a fundamental limitation of current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models because their restricted temporal context pre-vents effective accumulation and reuse of past experiences. As a result, memory has become a fundamental component for enabling embodied agents to perform long-horizon reasoning and adaptive decision-making.

This survey presents a systematic taxonomy of VLA memory mechanisms based on memory scope and persistence, categorizing existing approaches into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier.

Based on this taxonomy, we compare representative VLA memory systems in terms of memory characteristics, architectural com-plexity, and open-source maturity, revealing a clear trade-off in which increasing architectural complexity is generally accompanied by decreasing open-source ma-turity.

Finally, we discuss the key challenges in building full-lifecycle memory systems, including efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolu-tion. Overall, this survey provides a unified perspective on memory architectures for VLA agents and offers insights into the development of lifelong embodied in-telligence.

summary.en: This survey examines memory mechanisms for long-horizon robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models. It organizes existing approaches by memory scope and persistence into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier. The authors compare systems in memory characteristics, architectural complexity, and open-source maturity, reporting a general trade-off: greater architectural complexity tends to accompany lower open-source maturity. They also discuss challenges in efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolution.

sections.text:
A robot swarm covers a building faster with more robots, but the map is only as complete as the space the robots have physically visited. We target the amount of an unknown building a decentralized swarm knows at each instant, ahead of physical coverage.

SenseSwarm serves a lightweight learned map predictor on the swarm's shared occupancy map and folds the predicted structure back into a stigmergic guidance field. Its 709K-parameter predictor is fine-tuned on the swarm's own multi-front observations, which we show is necessary: a single-robot predictor collapses on such views.

We build a benchmark of twelve real building floors from HouseExpo, HKUST, and KTH, up to 24,000 square meters, and run 1,620 simulations across nine coordination methods, swarm sizes 32 to 512, and three seeds. On physical coverage the swarm is near parity with a greedy frontier planner, as expected.

On map reconstruction, every non-predictive baseline needs 1.3 to 1.9 times longer to reach an 80 percent known map, and SenseSwarm holds an equal-time area lead of about 670 square meters, up to 1,359.

Folding the prediction into the shared field matters: the same predictor applied per robot matches our speed but suffers a 6.9 times higher inter-robot contact rate at 512 robots. The prediction is computed once per shared map, so its cost stayed flat from 32 to 512 robots.

summary.en: SenseSwarm applies a lightweight learned map predictor to a swarm's shared occupancy map and incorporates predicted structure into a guidance field. The authors report a benchmark using twelve building floors from three sources and 1,620 simulations across nine coordination methods, swarm sizes, and seeds. In simulation, physical coverage is near parity with a greedy frontier planner, while map reconstruction reaches the stated known-map threshold faster than non-predictive baselines. Applying prediction per robot has a higher inter-robot contact rate at the largest tested swarm size.
summary.zh: SenseSwarm将轻量级学习式地图预测器用于群体共享占据地图，并把预测结构融入引导场，以估计机器人尚未实地覆盖的建筑空间。作者在来自三个数据集的12个真实建筑楼层上开展了1620次仿真，比较九种协调方法及不同群体规模。仿真中，实体覆盖表现接近贪心前沿规划器；地图重建更快达到已知地图比例目标。逐机器人使用预测器时，512台机器人规模下的接触率更高。

sections.text:
We introduce Accelerating Dexterity via Pre-Training (ADEPT), a large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning sim-to-real transferable dexterity across high degree-of-freedom (DoF) robot embodiments that can solve long-horizon tasks directly from raw visuo-tactile perception.

ADEPT pretrains a dexterous policy on a generic object reposing task, then post-trains downstream policies with this pretrained behavior as a prior. ADEPT enables learning new behaviors that are otherwise difficult to discover from scratch on multi-fingered robots and avoids learning the same set of skills over again for every new downstream task.

The pretrained policy zero-shots the reposing phase of downstream tasks, but na\"ive RL fine-tuning rapidly degrades this capability during transfer. We address this with a stable post-training recipe combining behavior-cloning distillation, critic warm-up, and conservative on-policy updates.

To safely exploit the full kinematic dexterity, we introduce a joint-space Geometric Fabric that mediates between the RL policy and the robot.

We distill post-trained teachers into perceptive students that zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on two embodiments: a 23 DoF Kuka-Allegro with two RGB cameras, and a 29 DoF Flexiv-Sharpa with two RGB cameras and five vision-based tactile sensors, and can solve long-horizon tasks from challenging initial states with dexterity at human-level speed.

summary.en: ADEPT is a reinforcement-learning framework that pretrains dexterous policies on a generic object-reposing task, then uses the learned behavior as a prior for downstream post-training. The authors say this can support behaviors that are difficult to discover from scratch. To limit capability loss during transfer, their post-training recipe combines behavior-cloning distillation, critic warm-up, and conservative on-policy updates. A joint-space Geometric Fabric mediates between policy and robot. Distilled perceptive students are reported to transfer zero-shot from simulation to two robot embodiments for long-horizon tasks.
summary.zh: ADEPT是一种强化学习框架，先在通用物体重新摆放任务上预训练灵巧操作策略，再将其作为先验用于下游任务后训练。作者称该方法有助于学习从零开始难以发现的行为，并通过行为克隆蒸馏、评论家预热和保守的在线策略更新，减少迁移时预训练能力退化。框架还使用关节空间Geometric Fabric协调策略与机器人。经蒸馏的感知学生策略在两种机器人构型上实现仿真到现实零样本迁移，并处理长时程任务。

items.title: ADEPT: Accelerating Dexterity via Pre-Training and Post-Training using Reinforcement Learning

sections.text:
Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural changes.

We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA.

Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse while mitigating interference.

Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld, ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation.

Code is available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA.

summary.en: NestedVLA addresses the difficulty of consolidating skills learned across tasks and environments by proposing independent skill learning followed by post hoc consolidation. A task-conditioned nested hypernetwork generates adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA, while compressed task-specific VLM residuals are stored separately. Across three reinforcement-learning benchmarks—MetaWorld, ManiSkill, and CALVIN—the authors report an average 41 percentage-point gain over the strongest model-merging baseline, performance within one point of per-task fine-tuning on ManiSkill, and a substantially reduced gap on CALVIN.

items.title: NestedVLA: Learning to Consolidate and Generate Skills for Vision-Language-Action Models

sections.text:
Learning from Observation (LfO) is a fundamental robotic capability that replicates how humans and animals socially learn from each other. Beyond its biological parallels, this modality provides a practical solution for data scaling in sample-inefficient and data-starved domains like robotics.

Recent work has demonstrated promising results in learning manipulation skills from human videos, yet progress in this area remains difficult to assess. Existing methods vary widely in assumptions, hardware choices, and environment setups making it difficult to draw meaningful comparisons and identify advances in the field.

To address these challenges, we introduce RoboReel: a unified benchmark for evaluating models that learn policies from human videos. RoboReel consists of bundled real-world human demonstration videos, simulated robot trajectories, and evaluation environments on ten manipulation tasks.

We develop four test suites to evaluate the models' performance on multiple axes, including the robustness to visual distractors and the ability to complete long-horizon tasks. We further validate RoboReel by recreating a subset of its tasks in the real world, showing that relative performance trends observed in simulation are preserved in the real world.

Our benchmark covers learning-from-observation models from different categories, and studies the effectiveness of multiple representation choices in our benchmark evaluation that covers over seven state-of-the-art algorithms (including our VLA based variants) in the field of LfO.

Finally, we present an analysis of the different types of algorithms showing that long-horizon tasks and tasks with low tolerances are still challenging for current models. Webpage: https://roboreel.github.io

summary.en: The paper introduces RoboReel, a unified benchmark for evaluating policies learned from human videos. It includes real-world human demonstrations, simulated robot trajectories, and evaluation environments for ten manipulation tasks. Four test suites assess capabilities such as robustness to visual distractors and long-horizon completion. The authors recreate some tasks in the real world and report that relative performance trends seen in simulation are preserved. The evaluation covers multiple model categories, representation choices, and more than seven algorithms; long-horizon and low-tolerance tasks remain challenging.

sections.text:
Precise pedicel-targeted grasping in strawberry harvesting remains a critical bottleneck due to the pedicel's small diameter (1.3-3 mm), color similarity with surrounding foliage, and precise force control required for clean abscission zone detachment.

As a market-grade crop, strawberry aesthetic value makes bruise-free pedicel detachment essential over direct fruit grasping. Classical approaches struggle to unify vision models, motion planning, and contact manipulation into a robust framework, particularly in occluded canopy environments.

Therefore, this work presents a visuomotor imitation learning pipeline for pedicel-targeted strawberry harvesting that unifies perception, motion planning, and contact manipulation from collecting human teleoperation demonstrations, training an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy with a ResNet-50 visual backbone, and deploying the learned policy autonomously on a Jetson AGX Orin edge platform at 15 Hz.

The trained policy achieved consistent loss convergence from 2.84 to 0.091 over 100K gradient steps on 130 demonstrations. We have also established a reproducible open-source pipeline with publicly released dataset and model weights for the agricultural robotics community.

Full dataset is available at, https://huggingface.co/datasets/nitindominicrai/strawberry_pedicel_grasp_teleoperation and trained policy at, https://huggingface.co/nitindominicrai/act_strawberry_pedicel.

To replicate this work, all code, configurations, and deployment instructions are publicly available at, https://github.com/nitin-dominic/autonomous_strawberry_pedicel_harvesting.

summary.en: The paper presents a visuomotor imitation-learning pipeline for strawberry harvesting that targets the pedicel for bruise-free detachment. It combines human teleoperation demonstrations with an Action Chunking with Transformers policy using a ResNet-50 visual backbone, deployed on a Jetson AGX Orin. The authors report that training on 130 demonstrations reduced loss from 2.84 to 0.091 over 100,000 gradient steps. They also describe a reproducible pipeline and publicly released data, weights, and deployment materials; the abstract does not report harvest success rates or field validation.

sections.text:
Manipulating deformable objects toward desired 3D configurations is a fundamental capability for robots operating in unstructured physical environments.

However, as the range of possible initial and target configurations grows, goal-conditioned deformable manipulation requires a robot to infer increasingly diverse manipulation behaviors in addition to precise continuous actions. We introduce DefFlow, a framework for goal-conditioned manipulation of deformable objects toward a broad range of 3D configurations.

DefFlow learns from demonstrations by jointly predicting the goal-conditioned 3D point flow of the robot and deformable object.

We show that this formulation better captures both the manipulation decisions, such as when and where to grasp, release, or re-grasp, and the precise continuous motions required for goal reaching, rather than predicting only the robot flow.

Across rope, granular-media, and cloth manipulation settings with diverse initial and target configurations, DefFlow substantially outperforms goal-conditioned action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines on success rates and goal-distance metrics.

We further demonstrate deployment of our framework on a real robot using real point-cloud observations and unseen goal configurations.

summary.en: The paper introduces DefFlow for manipulating deformable objects toward target 3D configurations. From demonstrations, it jointly predicts goal-conditioned 3D point flows for the robot and object, aiming to represent both decisions such as grasping, releasing, or re-grasping and the continuous motions needed to reach a goal. Across rope, granular-media, and cloth settings with varied initial and target configurations, the authors report higher success rates and better goal-distance metrics than goal-conditioned action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines. They also demonstrate deployment on a real robot with real point-cloud observations and unseen goals.

sections.text:
Learning effective action representations is critical for robotic manipulation, where raw control trajectories are often noisy, redundant, and difficult to model directly. Existing methods mainly encode the structure of the action stream itself, treating the role of actions in the environment as implicit.

Yet manipulation is about changing the world: the same action segment can induce different outcomes under different scene contexts, making action semantics inherently environment-dependent. We propose EDAR, an Environment-Dependent Action Representation that grounds action tokens in both executable control structure and expected visual consequences.

By coupling motor commands with their environment-conditioned effects, EDAR encourages the learned action space to capture interaction semantics rather than merely command-level patterns. Experiments on simulated and real-robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that EDAR improves downstream policy learning, especially in long-horizon manipulation.

These results highlight the importance of grounding action representations in executable control structure and environment-conditioned visual change.

summary.en: The paper proposes EDAR, an action representation method that grounds action tokens in executable control structure and expected visual consequences. It is designed to capture how actions affect the world in a particular scene, rather than encoding command patterns alone. Experiments on simulated and real-robot manipulation benchmarks show improved downstream policy learning, especially for long-horizon manipulation. The authors emphasize grounding representations in control structure and environment-conditioned visual change; the abstract provides no specific magnitude for the reported improvements.

Multi-robot authoring can reduce completion time by distributing drawing work, but the resulting speedup depends on task structure and the allocation-routing pipeline.

We investigate these relationships by representing drawings as geometric stroke graphs and comparing component-level (single-token) allocation with shared-token (decomposed) allocation, which permits multiple robots to work within a connected component.

A simulation study of 385 drawings and teams of one to eight robots shows diminishing speedup gains under single-token allocation and larger mean speedups under the shared-token pipeline, each normalized by its own single-robot completion time.

Shared-token execution also exhibits lower idle-time shares at larger team sizes, although it does not reduce completion time for every drawing. Comparisons across structural attribute groups reveal associations between structural descriptors and differences in scaling behavior, with greater separation between several attribute groups at larger team sizes.

These findings characterize empirical scaling in the evaluated pipelines and highlight the importance of considering within-component workload and graph structure alongside component count. Additional materials are available at https://sites.google.com/view/multirobotauthoring/home.

Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera.

Trustworthy robot behavior requires not only high levels of task success but also that the robot can reliably quantify how likely it is to succeed.

Traditional methods plan feasible paths for multiple agents in the stochastic environment. However, the methods' iterations with the changes in the environment result in computation complexities, especially for the decentralized agents without a centralized planner.

Although reinforcement learning provides a plausible solution because of the generalization for different environments, it struggles with enormous agent-environment interactions in training.

Here, we propose a novel centralized training with decentralized execution method based on multi-agent reinforcement learning, which is improved based on the idea of model predictive control. In our approach, agents communicate only with the centralized planner to make decentralized decisions online in the stochastic environment.

Furthermore, considering the communication constraint with the centralized planner, each agent plans feasible paths through the extended observation, which combines information on neighboring agents based on the distance-weighted mean field approach.

Inspired by the rolling optimization approach of model predictive control, we conduct multi-step value convergence in multi-agent reinforcement learning to enhance the training efficiency, which reduces the expensive interactions in convergence.

Experiment results in both comparison, ablation, and real-robot studies validate the effectiveness and generalization performance of our method.

Legged robots equipped with manipulators offer promising capabilities for loco-manipulation tasks in unstructured environments.

However, achieving task-consistent end-effector behavior during locomotion remains challenging due to terrain-induced disturbances and the strong coupling between locomotion and manipulation, particularly for small-scale quadruped platforms.

A reinforcement-learning based whole-body control framework is proposed for quadruped loco-manipulation on complex terrain. The proposed framework combines a hybrid task representation with task-prioritized whole-body learning to coordinate locomotion and manipulation while preserving task-consistent end-effector behavior.

Automating biological laboratories requires robots to perform dexterous tool interactions under realistic visual conditions while handling dynamic experimental phenomena, presenting significant challenges for robotic manipulation.

To enable systematic evaluation under these conditions, we introduce DexBioLab, a simulation benchmark and framework for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments.

DexBioLab comprises 14 tasks across 4 robot embodiments, spanning functional tool use, precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation. We introduce controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor, and bubbles, to capture the evolving visual conditions of laboratory procedures.

To further enhance environmental realism, we develop a hybrid rendering pipeline that integrates interactive simulated foreground objects with Gaussian-splatting backgrounds reconstructed from 6 real laboratory scenes.

Our evaluation reveals substantial variation in policy performance across tasks, exposing distinct strengths and weaknesses of current manipulation policies. Real-world experiments further demonstrate a reduced sim-to-real gap, supporting the validity of AutoBio+ for realistic manipulation evaluation.

The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet robot planning often benefits from hybrid discrete-continuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes or discrete primitive actions.

Existing methods typically rely on human-defined symbol sets or symbols derived from language supervision, without asking what makes a symbol computationally useful. In this paper, we take an inference-algorithm--centric view to define usefulness: a good symbol should expose the discrete commitments that simplify solving the original planning problem.

We first introduce the concept of solver-sufficient symbolization by studying finite-horizon piecewise-affine systems, for which solver sufficiency can be precisely characterized, and develop a counterexample-guided algorithm for symbol invention.

We then extend this principle to invent symbols for optimization objectives parameterized by general neural networks as energy functions, showing that solver-sufficient symbols can nevertheless be induced from their continuous optimization landscapes.

Experiments on simulated and real-robot tasks show that the resulting symbols reduce solving cost while preserving solution quality, while also improving interpretability and steerability. Furthermore, our theoretical and algorithmic insights help explain why certain human-defined symbols are computationally useful.

We investigate whether coding agents can automate this design process through iterative implementation and evaluation. Under a fixed development budget, a Designer Agent writes and revises code for memory construction and retrieval using feedback from a fixed Query Agent.

These results demonstrate the potential of coding agents to automate spatial memory design, while revealing task-dependent trade-offs in performance and computational cost.

Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) inherit their visual and linguistic capabilities from Vision-Language Models (VLMs), yet most VLAs are built from off-the-shelf VLMs that are not adapted to the embodied domain, limiting their downstream performance. In this work, we propose EmbodiedMidtrain to bridge the gap between VLMs and VLAs.

We first characterize the data distribution gap between them, showing that VLA data occupy compact regions that are largely separated from the broader VLM distribution, while the degree of alignment varies substantially both across and within VLM data sources.

Then, we build a mid-training data engine that leverages a lightweight learnable proximity estimator to select the most VLA-aligned candidates from a large VLM pool, and produce EmbodiedMidtrain-1M, a VLM dataset that we further use to mid-train the VLM before downstream VLA fine-tuning.

Experiments on both simulated robot manipulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show consistent VLA performance gains over off-the-shelf checkpoints across VLM backbones and VLA action heads. These gains extend to downstream tasks not used to guide data selection.

Further analysis reveals that mid-training provides a stronger initialization for VLA fine-tuning, with gains emerging from the earliest steps and widening throughout training.

Moreover, the data engine captures both dataset-level and sample-level alignment signals, favoring spatial reasoning over text-centric tasks while preserving the diversity of the VLM data. We will release all code, data and models for future research.

Robots performing long-horizon visual manipulation observe high-dimensional images, but successful plans depend on action-relevant facts: what can be done now and what changes afterward. A useful planning representation should discard irrelevant visual details while preserving action applicability and effects.

Classical task planners exploit this structure through symbolic operators with preconditions and effects, but obtaining such representations from raw visual experience remains challenging. We study a visual task-planning setting in which a robot receives only image transitions: the current image, executed high-level action, and the resulting image.

At test time, given a start image and a goal image, the robot must produce a sequence of high-level actions that reaches the goal. To address this problem, we introduce STRIPS-WM, a framework for learning image-grounded STRIPS-style world models directly from visual transitions.

STRIPS-WM first induces a finite abstract transition graph from images, then learns latent binary predicates and one grounded propositional operator per action label. The learned operators form a symbolic action model with sparse preconditions and add/delete effects.

Finally, the learned predicates are distilled into a visual encoder, enabling classical planning directly from novel start and goal images. Experiments on visual rearrangement tasks show that STRIPS-WM improves image-to-plan success over the tested visual rollout, latent graph-search and latent-symbolic baselines.

How can pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models retain long-horizon visual histories with high-frequency updates without sacrificing efficiency? Existing approaches rely on external memory management, which restrains either the memory horizon or the reactiveness of pretrained policies.

To this end, we present NativeMEM, a VLA policy that features long-term and real-time updated memory. At its core is an efficient memory encoding scheme, Native Memory Compression, which repurposes the VLA's own vision encoder to compress each historical frame from each camera view into a single token.

Appended to the input sequence, these memory tokens enable the pretrained VLA to attend over long-term history with negligible latency overhead, requiring neither an external planner nor a freshly initialized memory module.

sections.text:
Robot manipulators often come into contact with rigid objects when performing work. This imposes physical constraints on their motion. Simultaneous force & motion control was developed to regulate contact forces commensurate with these constraints, whilst projecting motion control in to the orthogonal, unconstrained directions.

This is typically formulated in the task coordinates, i.e. operational space, then mapped to joint torques to command the robot. However, most constraints on the robot control, such as joint limits, collision avoidance, singularity avoidance, etc. are naturally expressed in generalised coordinates (joint space).

Thus, formulating the control problem in task space makes it difficult to guarantee control feasibility. In this paper Gauss' principle of least constraint is used to solve the control as a quadratic programming (QP) problem in generalised coordinates.

It is shown that the theoretical solution to this problem produces the correct constrained dynamics for accurate contact force control. Moreover, inequality constraints may be appended to ensure feasibility and safety. Simulation results were conducted in MuJoCo and compared to the operational space formulation.

The proposed method is able to simultaneously maintain a desired contact force, minimise trajectory tracking error, and adhere to practical inequality constraints.

items.title: Simultaneous Force and Motion Control in Generalised Coordinates
